155-the-moonstone:
A great yellow diamond, stolen from an Indian shrine, brings ruin to an English house. Wilkie Collins's Moonstone, told in eight narratives, opens with the storming of Seringapatam in 1799 and the gem's curse. Rachel Verinder receives the stone on her birthday, then it vanishes in the night.

Betteredge the steward, Sergeant Cuff, and lovers Franklin Blake and Rachel each tell part of the tale. Opium, a painted door, and a second theft twist the plot toward truth. Collins builds suspense from conflicting views rather than one voice. The novel founded the modern detective story.
19703-madame-delphine:
George W. Cable wrote about Creole New Orleans with unmatched local knowledge. Madame Delphine is one of his best-known stories of that city. Its opening shows a quarter sunk into long decay. Old commercial glory has shrunk into small shops. Bright market stalls stand out like patches of mould. Cable sets mood before he sets plot in motion.

Cable's New Orleans tales deal with caste, color, and old French families. Madame Delphine stands at the center of such a tale. Her story turns on sacrifice within a rigid social order. Cable wrote the city's speech and streets from life. His work helped define Southern local-color fiction. This short novel remains a fine place to meet it.
19779-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-20-no-:
The Atlantic Monthly for August 1867 is volume 20, number 118 of the magazine. One essay here treats grief with striking practicality. Grief, it says, must be fed with thought or starve to death. The best plan is keeping the mind busy with other work. The essay calls busyness a spiritual anesthetic for sorrow. Such counsel filled postwar American magazines.

The Civil War had ended two years before this issue. Its readers knew bereavement at national scale. The Atlantic mixed essays, fiction, and reviews for educated households. A single issue preserves the era's whole mental diet. Scholars read such numbers to hear 1867 thinking aloud. This one speaks in a Boston accent, thoughtful and composed.
19939-history-of-the-missions-of-the-ame:
This history covers missions of the American Board of Commissioners for Foreign Missions. Its ground is the Ottoman world: Armenians, Greeks, and the Turkish empire. In March 1846, Sir Stratford Canning reported from Constantinople. Thirty-six evangelical Armenians stood persecuted by their Patriarch, he wrote. Canning added personal efforts to soften their treatment. Diplomacy and missions intertwine through the narrative.

The American Board sent its first missionaries abroad in 1812. Its Near East missions built schools, presses, and colleges. Armenian converts stood at the center of this volume's story. Persecution reports shaped American sympathy and policy. The history is both record and advocacy. Scholars of missions still work through its documents.
19941-with-our-army-in-palestine:
John Morecroft wrote With Our Army in Palestine about the British campaign there. He corrects the home public's short version of that war. Most people think the Great Crusade began with taking Jerusalem, he says. They think it ended when the Turks surrendered in autumn 1918. That view is entirely erroneous, he insists. The campaign was longer, wider, and harder than the famous dates suggest.

Palestine saw fighting from Gaza to Damascus over two years. Allenby's army mixed British, Indian, Australian, and Arab forces. Morecroft marched with them as an official observer and writer. His book restores the campaign's full length. Desert, water, and distance are its real antagonists. It is solid campaign history from a participant.
19996-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-16-no-:
The Atlantic Monthly for October 1865 is volume 16, number 96. The Civil War had ended six months before this issue. One article attacks a fashionable claim about American health. Physical decay, it is said, threatens the American people. Unwise stimulation of the brain gets the blame. A deficiency of physical health in America is assumed as an axiom. The writer questions that assumption sharply. Postwar nerves were a national topic that autumn.

The magazine now spoke for a victorious, grieving Union. Its pages balanced reconstruction politics with science and letters. Health anxiety ran through much postwar writing. This article shows the argument in its first form. A single number captures the culture re-sorting itself. Scholars still read these volumes as America's diary.
20071-sue-a-little-heroine:
L. T. Meade wrote Sue, A Little Heroine, one of her many books for young readers. Sue is a small girl with a freckled face and red-tinged hair. Her eyes are bright blue and keen, the book notes at once. She pushes through a crowd to hear a street preacher speak.

A rough man lays a hand on her shoulder in that crowd. From such small scenes, Meade builds a tale of a brave child. Sue faces hard city life with faith and pluck. Readers get a Victorian tale of poverty, courage, and a child's good heart under strain.
20263-boswell-s-correspondence-with-the-:
James Boswell's correspondence with Andrew Erskine appears here with notes by George Birkbeck Hill. Hill praises a young Scot who dared to tour Corsica's interior. No traveler from Britain had visited that interior before him. Turkish corsairs still swarmed the Mediterranean in that risky age.

Corsica itself sat in a very unsettled state at the time. Boswell's letters show his wit, ambition, and love of great men. Erskine, a poet and soldier, proved a bright partner in letters. Readers get lively eighteenth-century correspondence, richly framed by a top editor.
20340-a-little-maid-of-old-maine:
Alice Turner Curtis wrote A Little Maid of Old Maine, a tale of the Revolution. Two girls carry a big basket toward the Machias River in Maine. It is a pleasant May morning in 1775, full of pine scent. Freshly cut logs have been poled downriver to the big sawmills.

War news from Lexington has just reached the Maine coast that spring. Machias would soon fight one of the first naval battles of the war. Curtis sets her little maid amid lumber, ships, and patriots. Young readers get Maine's own Revolution story, told at a child's height.
20378-christmas-sunshine:
Christmas Sunshine is a seasonal gift book of verse and readings for the Christmas season. Its pages mix classic religious poetry with pieces on winter, snow, and the birth of Christ. The selection suits family reading by the fireside.

One passage praises winter as it hides the bare earth under innocent snow. It speaks of a saintly veil of maiden white thrown over the year's shame. Such lines show the book's mix of nature writing and devotion, and the warmth its makers hoped to bring into the home at Christmas.
20496-legends-of-the-rhine:
Legends of the Rhine brings the old tales of Germany's great river to English-speaking readers. Castles, knights, water spirits, and doomed lovers crowd its pages. The book mixes travel talk with the legends themselves, in the manner of a journey up the river.

One scene has a young woman smile at a compliment to her mother. The mother, it turns out, was English by birth. The traveler remarks that Germany is the land of romance for the English, just as Italy is for the Germans. The legends that follow show why the Rhine earned that name.
20513-how-to-succeed-or-stepping-stones-:
Orison Swett Marden's How to Succeed, published in 1896, is one of the founding books of the success movement. Its full title promises stepping stones to fame and fortune. Marden told young readers that will and character, not luck, make a life.

Do not look far for the successful man, he writes. This man is you, it is I, it is each one of us. How do we constitute ourselves men? Nothing is harder if we do not know how to will it, and nothing easier if we will it. Such bracing talk made Marden's books steady sellers.
20616-the-old-front-line:
John Masefield walked the Somme battlefield soon after the fighting and wrote The Old Front Line about what he found. Masefield had served in France and wrote with a poet's eye. The book describes the trenches, villages, and graves of the 1916 battle.

He looks ahead to peace. The ground full of death will grow food again, he writes, and this frontier of trouble will be forgotten. When the trenches are filled in and the plough has gone over them, the land will not long keep the look of war. The book became a classic of battlefield writing.
21027-the-trial-of-charles-random-de-ber:
False word of peace with France, spread to lift the funds, charges the Crown in this trial. Charles de Berenger, Lord Cochrane, and others stood accused of that fraud in 1814. The Trial records a plot to make the king and public believe peace was near.

Stock Exchange fraud, a fake colonel, and a staged ride from Dover fill the case. Cochrane, a sea hero, swore his innocence to his death's door. The verdict wrecked his career, though later ages cleared his name in part. Trial reports like this preserve court drama word for word, cross-talk, proof, and all.
21119-flaming-june:
A tidy elderly spinster in a seaside town keeps a large house. It has private access to a shared garden, and her settled life is upset by a visitor. Her brother, now rich in America, sends his daughter Cornelia to England as part of her education. Cornelia arrives with plenty of pocket money and American habits.

Mrs George de Horne Vaizey sets the girl among polished, well-bred people who expect chaperones and strict manners. Cornelia gads about with young men as she pleases, to her aunt's dismay. The aunt proves right in the end: among all the nice people hides one bad character, revealed only near the close.
21250-sir-walter-scott-a-lecture-at-the-:
William Paton Ker delivered this lecture on Sir Walter Scott at the Sorbonne on May 22, 1919, in the Louis Liard series. He takes his text from Scott's own account of seeing Ivanhoe turned into an opera at the Odéon in Paris. Scott, who dictated much of that novel in pain at Abbotsford, marvelled that it now amused a foreign crowd.

Ker contrasts Scott's regional Scotland, its dialect barely clear outside its own ground, with the Europe-wide market that fought for his novels. The lecture first appeared in the Anglo-French Review in August 1919. It is a short, warm weighing of Scott's European fame.
21273-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-2-no-1:
The Atlantic Monthly for December 1858, volume two, number fourteen, opens with an essay on the ideal tendency in art. Its writer argues that art is the largest expression, pointing toward what cannot be measured or lodged in systems. Shakespeare, Plato, Michelangelo, Beethoven, and Goethe stand as its witnesses.

The young Atlantic, founded in Boston the year before, aimed to lead American letters, art, and politics in one magazine. A single monthly number like this one mixes essays, stories, poems, and reviews by the New England circle. Kept whole, it shows the magazine in its second year, when its table of contents was itself an argument about American culture.
21288-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-17-no-:
The Atlantic Monthly for March 1866, volume seventeen, number 101, leads with passages from Hawthorne's notebooks, published two years after his death. One entry describes a July 1837 drive near Augusta, Maine, to fish for white perch through a crooked, winding brook. The pilot talks politics and the bank between hearty tugs at a whiskey bottle.

Several dozen fish, yellow perch, a great chub, and horned pouts come home in an hour or two. Ticknor and Fields published the magazine in Boston as a monthly of literature, science, art, and politics. A single issue preserves its post-Civil War table, where Hawthorne's private journals shared space with the day's essays.
21325-outlines-of-greek-and-roman-medici:
James Sands Elliott was a New Zealand doctor and editor of the New Zealand Medical Journal. He wrote these outlines after a stay in southeastern Europe stirred his interest. Published in 1914, the book traces the main stages of healing in the Greek and Roman worlds. Those are the two empires to which modern civilisation owes most. Asklepios, the Greek god of healing, fronts it.

Elliott complains that the history of medicine is much neglected, even by doctors, so that many discoveries are only rediscoveries. He keeps the book a general outline rather than a full treatise, leaning on German historians like Baas and Sprengel. It serves as a short, readable first map of ancient medicine.
21408-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-17-no-:
The April 1866 number of the Atlantic Monthly, volume seventeen, number one hundred and two, leads with the last days of Walter Savage Landor. Landor had died at Florence in September 1864, and many readers barely knew his name. The piece asks why so bright a writer was so little read.

The Atlantic was then a leading magazine of letters, science, art, and public life. Its pages mixed essays, reviews, poems, and tales for a broad, keen readership. This number preserves a slice of that world just after the Civil War. Emerson's own account of Landor, from English Traits, is quoted and weighed.
21572-percival-keene:
Percival Keene grows up near Southampton in Captain Marryat's novel of 1842, his nineteenth book. An old mansion house, known by its name for centuries, stands a few miles from the town. Sea service, in the channel frigate world of the day, shapes the hero's path.

Channel service, Marryat jokes, meant a captain with a seat in Parliament. His frigate rarely went to sea while the House was sitting, lest his vote be missed. Against that sly background, young Keene learns the navy as it truly was. Love, patronage, and action fill a tale told with Marryat's usual pace and humour.
21642-lady-cadogan-s-illustrated-games-o:
Lady Cadogan's Illustrated Games of Solitaire, in a new revised edition of 1914, adds American games. David McKay of Philadelphia issued the book, under the motto that patience conquers. A line from Othello asks how poor are they that have not patience.

Terms come first: foundation cards, suitable cards, and marriage, meaning a card placed on its neighbour in suit. Games run from Canfield, or Klondike, to Napoleon at St Helena and the Besieged City. La Belle Lucie, the Flower Garden, and the Sultan crowd the long contents list. Players get clear rules and pictures for dozens of single-player card games.
21716-the-battery-and-the-boiler-adventu:
A baby born at sea in a howling storm grows up to work with the newest wonder of his age in this Ballantyne tale. The boy's early squalls mark him, the ship's cook jokes, as one who will make his mark somehow. He finds his chance in the laying of submarine telegraph cables, the wires that first linked lands across the oceans.

Ballantyne studied cable laying firsthand, as he did for many of his books on trades and crafts. Storms, ships, sparks, and mishaps fill the story, mixing sea adventure with early electrical work. Readers get a lively look at the crews who strung the world's first ocean telegraph lines.
22058-cornelius-o-dowd-upon-men-and-wome:
Charles Lever, the Irish novelist, created Cornelius O'Dowd as a comic mask for his magazine essays. The pieces first ran in Blackwood's Magazine and were gathered in book form in 1864. O'Dowd introduces himself as a man who waited fourteen years at levees for government favour. No viceroy ever gave him a post, which leaves him free to talk.

From Italian battlefields to Dublin drawing rooms, O'Dowd comments on everything. Garibaldi's worshippers, Solferino, Italian law, and organ grinders all come under his eye. The humour is broad, Irish, and topical. Readers in the 1860s took these papers as light relief with a sting.
22090-the-task-of-social-hygiene:
Havelock Ellis, the English writer on sex and society, set out his programme in The Task of Social Hygiene. Ellis says social hygiene grows out of the older idea of social reform, but goes deeper. Reform treated bad conditions as they arose. Hygiene, as he defines it, aims at prevention: finding the source of social ills before they take hold.

Ellis discusses the family, birth, education, and the health of the race. Some of his views carry the stamp of his age's faith in eugenics, which readers now judge harshly. Others look ahead to public health and planned welfare. The book is a clear statement of how one Edwardian thinker hoped science would remake society.
22097-byeways-in-palestine:
James Finn served as British consul in Jerusalem through the middle of the nineteenth century. His Byeways in Palestine gathers journeys off the beaten road of the Holy Land. Finn admits he carried no fine instruments, only sometimes a common thermometer. He had no time for digging or surveying; his consular work came first.

What he offers instead is close knowledge of the country and its peoples. Fellahin villages, Bedouin camps, Samaritan and Jewish communities all appear. Finn notices crops, ruins, customs, and quarrels with a resident's eye. The book is a useful record of Ottoman Palestine before tourists and archaeologists remade the picture of it.
22245-steve-and-the-steam-engine:
Sara Ware Bassett wrote Steve and the Steam Engine in 1921, a boys' novel with a railroad heart. Steve begins the book in disgrace. While his parents were in New York and the chauffeur lay in hospital, he took the family's big six-cylinder car without permission. He carried a crowd of friends to a football game at Torrington, and that, the narrator warns, was not the worst of it.

To earn back trust, Steve is sent to work where steam engines rule. Bassett's Cape Cod tales usually smell of salt water; here coal smoke takes over. The book teaches railroad practice inside a story of a boy making good. It is wholesome series fiction of the post-war years.
22317-george-bowring-a-tale-of-cader-idr:
George Bowring is R. D. Blackmore's tale of Cader Idris, drawn from Slain by the Doones. Cader Idris is the great Welsh mountain of legend. The story, though, opens with school days and a sudden parting.

Within a week, George and the narrator were forced to leave their school. They left the grand old town and the lovely Severn too. All they kept was one another. That loss hangs over the tale from its first pages. Blackmore blends boyhood friendship with Welsh mountain country. Readers get a short, fond, sorrowful story from a writer best known for the wilder Doone country nearby.
22470-the-bell-tone:
Edmund H. Leftwich wrote The Bell Tone, a science fiction story of alien signals. Its narrator studies a wave used for sending thought images. The wave measures .00176 meter, he reports with care.

Pictures may be sent with a clacking code or independently. The narrator can conceive no finer communications system than this. He resolves that he must learn their secret methods fully. That hunger to decode drives the tale's investigation of contact. Thought pictures cross space by tone in his account. Readers get an inventor's-eye tale of first contact by signal. It prizes clever decoding over battles or chases in space.
22511-rollo-on-the-rhine:
Jacob Abbott wrote Rollo on the Rhine for his famous Rollo travel series. Rollo tours Europe with his family, learning geography as he goes. This volume follows the great Rhine river country of Germany.

Abbott first explains how mountain waters find the sea. Thousands of smaller torrents unite into larger and larger streams. At length they make four mighty rivers of Europe. Streams of the southern slopes form one great river, the Po. It flows east into the Adriatic Sea, he teaches. Such lessons precede the castles and towns of the Rhine itself. Young readers learned Europe's rivers through a boy's journey. Abbott's calm, instructive voice made the series a household standard.
22833-alcyone:
Vast, empty space opens Alcyone, a long poem named for a bright star. Its opening crosses a lifeless waste where night rules alone, vast and still. Nothing lives there now. Only the crumbled remains of ancient worlds lie scattered through the silence.

From that cosmic graveyard the poem ranges over time, death, and the fate of worlds. Its manner is grand and solemn, closer to meditation than to story. Readers should expect sweeping questions rather than characters. The verse belongs to a period when astronomy fed poetry, and new knowledge of deep space stirred awe as much as fear. Alcyone preserves that awe in period dress.
23005-eli-first-published-in-the-century:
A boat needs painting in Eli, Heman White Chaplin's story first published in the Century Magazine. A boy comes down to the shore, and his father rises, surveying the green bottom of the boat. Mother sent word that dinner is ready, the father guesses. He must eat fast, he says, and finish painting the boat's far side before the tide turns.

Tide rules everything in Chaplin's fishing world, even dinner. His Eli is built from such small, true pressures, work against water, hunger against duty. The dialect stays light on the page and exact to the ear. Stories like this one made his name in the great magazines. They preserve the speech and labor of the New England shore, net by net and coat of paint by coat.
23006-five-hundred-dollars-first-publish:
Captains swap a story in Five Hundred Dollars, Heman White Chaplin's tale first published in the Century Magazine. Captain Bennett opens the yarn by recalling David Prince's whaling voyage on the Viola. Captain Philo agrees that Prince's departure, at the time, looked suspiciously hurried. With most anyone else, he'd have thought something was up.

Whaling money and a hurried departure promise the rest. Chaplin lets two old sailors unfold the tale at harbor pace, hint by hint. Five hundred dollars, the title's sum, hangs over Prince's voyage from the first exchange. The frame is half the pleasure, gnarled narrators weighing a younger man's luck. It is a yarn in the true sense, spun dockside.
23007-the-village-convict-first-publishe:
Snow crunches at the store door in The Village Convict, Heman White Chaplin's story first published in the Century Magazine. Trade's looking up, William, Captain Seth tells the storekeeper, as someone kicks snow off his boots on the doorstep. Somebody's found he's got to have a shoestring before morning, he jokes.

Inside that warm store waits the village's judgment on a man marked by prison. Chaplin's convict returns to a place where everyone knows his record and measures his worth by his work. The story asks how much mercy a small town keeps in stock. Its setting does quiet argument, neighbors talking a man's fate over in the ordinary run of trade. Chaplin handles the question without preaching.
23040-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-18-no-:
The Atlantic Monthly for August 1866 argues about reunion. One essay imagines a statesman nearly despairing of the South after four years of war. Can anything good come from that quarter, he wonders. Yet a small, bright spot now shows at the Carolina cloud's very edge.

Hope and suspicion share this number, as they shared the country. Around the political essays sit poems, fiction, and reviews from the magazine's strong bench. The Atlantic stood at the center of American letters, and a monthly number shows its range in a single binding. August 1866 catches the nation mid-argument about what the war had settled. The spider's golden and silver silk of one image becomes, hopefully, a bond of union.
23108-chester-rand-or-the-new-path-to-fo:
Silas Tripp keeps the store in Chester Rand, or The New Path to Fortune. Silas Tripp may be Wyncombe's best-known citizen, the narrator figures. He runs the store in that Pennsylvania mountain village, lodges travelers in three spare rooms, serves as town treasurer, and fills other local offices besides.

Against Tripp's settled standing, young Chester Rand must find his path. Horatio Alger wrote this tale of a boy's rise, and its machinery is his, a good lad, a rich man to impress, luck that rewards virtue exactly on schedule. Store, town office, and mountain town fill the stage. Readers get the Alger formula in working order, cheerful, moral, and sure that fortune favors the deserving.
23137-diary-in-america-series-one:
Travelers contradict each other in Diary in America, series one. Talented travelers described the same nation in wildly clashing ways, the diarist marvels. Their harvests of fact, he adds, were generally meager for all their talent. The judgments pronounced on America, and pronounced so unjust by Americans, excited his curiosity.

Captain Frederick Marryat, the naval novelist, crossed the Atlantic to see for himself in the late 1830s. His diary records steamboats, prisons, elections, and manners with a sailor's bluntness. America fascinated and exasperated him by turns. Marryat's diary stands among the sharpest of the many British travel books on the young republic. Its author sized up a whole country with a naval officer's eye.
23246-mistress-anne:
Temple Bailey's Mistress Anne is a novel that opens in the afterglow of the holidays. The second day of the New Year fell on a Saturday, stretching the festive mood across the whole weekend. Wreaths from Christmas still hung in the windows. There had been an extra day of feasting, too.

Holidays always brought people in from town, Bailey notes, and they ate with sharp appetites. That warm, well-fed household sets the stage for Anne's story. Readers get a gentle period novel of home, guests, and manners, where small social moments carry the weight of the plot.
23292-ted-and-the-telephone:
Sara Ware Bassett's Ted and the Telephone, from 1922, is set in Freeman's Falls. Ted Turner lives in that sleepy New Hampshire town, beside a small river. Cotton mills stand in the town, and without them, Bassett notes, there would probably be no town at all.

The mills were not drawn to the town; the town arose because of the mills. That plain fact shapes Ted's world of work, family, and small-town ties. Readers get a novel of mill-town life in which a telephone, still a modern device, gives the story its title and its spark.
267-the-touchstone:
Stephen Glennard, a struggling New York writer, owns letters from a dead novelist who once loved him. Edith Wharton's Touchstone follows Glennard as he sells Margaret Aubyn's letters to pay for his marriage. Professor Joslin's newspaper appeal for Aubyn papers opens the tale.

Glennard's wife Alexa learns the source of their comfort, and his conscience sharpens. Wharton weighs love, money, and literary honor in a short, tense novel. The touchstone of the title tests character, not gold. The book shows Wharton's moral irony at full strength. Wharton's short novel pairs well with her longer studies of Old New York.
309-rhymes-of-a-rolling-stone:
Robert W. Service, the rolling stone himself, spatters seas of ink and asks the gods' pardon. Rhymes of a Rolling Stone, in the 1912 edition printed in 1917, opens with a prelude on literary sins. The contents run from A Rolling Stone to The Wanderlust.

Poems cover soldiers of fortune, gramophones at Fond-du-Lac, Athabaska Dick, and a trapper's Christmas Eve. The Lunger, the Quitter, and the Cow-Juice Cure mix comedy with frontier hardship. Service's rolling verse carries readers from Yukon to prairie. The book shows his range beyond gold-rush fame.
327-the-princess-aline:
Princess Aline of Hohenwald enters Morton Carlton's life exactly when his heart and time stand free. Richard Harding Davis's Princess Aline follows Morney Carlton, a rich young New Yorker, through wise and foolish deeds for love. Had she come sooner or later, she might have passed unnoticed.

Carlton can look back with modest satisfaction and forward with pleasure, yet Aline unsettles both. Davis mixes European courts, American wealth, and romantic comedy. The novella's charm lies in timing: love arrives at the one open moment. It remains a light Davis favorite.
403-soldiers-of-fortune:
Richard Harding Davis sets this romance in New York drawing rooms and a South American revolt. Alice Langham meets a rough westerner at a dinner party, then finds him again as a soldier of fortune abroad. Reginald King, a polished rival, offers wealth and ease, while the westerner offers danger and a cause.

Davis writes bright society scenes, then shifts to jungle camps, plots, and a fight for a small republic. Love and loyalty test Alice at each turn. The novel charms as a dashing tale of its age, where a woman must choose between safe comfort and a man who lives by risk.
490-life-and-adventures-of-calamity-jane:
Martha Cannary, known as Calamity Jane, tells her own life in this brief memoir, written in her own rough voice. Born in Princeton, Missouri, in 1852, she rode horses young, crossed to Montana by wagon in 1865, and won fame as a shot and fearless rider. Scouts, camps, and frontier towns fill her pages.

Jane writes plainly of hunts, river crossings, and hard trails, with little polish and much pluck. Scholars debate how much is tall tale, but the voice rings true to her legend. The memoir endures as a frontier self-portrait, brisk, boastful, and full of dust, danger, and pride.
497-tracks-of-a-rolling-stone:
Henry Coke recalls a wandering life in this memoir, written in five months without diary or notes. Coke, a younger son with little fortune, roams schools, clubs, and continents, telling tales of friends, duels, and scrapes. A second edition adds fresh stories after readers welcomed the first.

Coke writes with easy, anecdotal charm, opening on how little we recall our own childhood. His tracks cross Victorian high life and low adventure alike. The memoir charms as a gentleman's ramble through a vanished age, where a rolling stone gathers more tales than moss.
69-the-32nd-mersenne-prime-predicted-by-:
Prime numbers of the form two to a power minus one have lured hunters for centuries. This file records the 32nd Mersenne prime, found by David Slowinski and published in honor of Andrew Wiles's proof of Fermat's Last Theorem. The note dates the find to February 1993.

Computing the giant number took about 26.56 minutes on a four-processor Cray-2 running Maple. The bulk of the file is the prime itself, printed in long digit blocks. Readers can check its size and form against the Mersenne list. The file stands as a raw artifact of early supercomputer number hunting.
747-anomalies-and-curiosities-of-medicin:
George M. Gould and Walter L. Pyle compiled this vast medical reference on the strange and rare in human bodies and disease. Drawn from journals and case reports, it gathers accounts of giants and dwarfs, extra limbs, long life, strange births, and freaks of nature, each with its source noted. The scale is huge, running to thousands of cases.

The doctors present each case in sober, clinical prose, sorting wonders from frauds where they can. The book was meant for physicians, yet it fascinates lay readers too. It stands as a monument of Victorian medical curiosity, and as a record of what doctors saw, believed, and tried to explain before modern genetics.
748-the-brother-of-daphne:
Dornford Yates wrote this light comedy about Daphne and her brother, told with wit and a keen eye for manners. Chapters with titles such as Punch and Judy, Clothes and the Man, and The Judgement of Paris set the tone: social games, love scenes, and points of honour played for laughs. Daphne, at ease in her long chair, spars with the narrator from the first page.

Yates moves his people through parties, pictures, and country houses, where pride comes before a fall and love scenes turn on a word. The humour is urbane and a touch mischievous, never cruel. The book charms readers who enjoy a well-bred farce, where charm and cheek carry the day and all is found out in the end.
788-the-red-one:
Jack London gathered four tales in this 1919 volume, headed by the title story of Bassett, a sick man in the Solomon Islands. Bassett hears a vast, unearthly sound rolling from a mountain gorge, a peal he likens to an archangel's trump, and he strives to trace it to its source. The other tales follow in the same Pacific world.

The Hussy, Like Argus of the Ancient Times, and The Princess turn on love, fate, and the clash of white men and island peoples. London writes with his usual force, though the title tale leans toward mystery and awe. The book shows his late work at its most strange and haunting, far from the Yukon of his fame.
819-the-history-of-the-telephone:
Herbert N. Casson wrote this history of the telephone just thirty-five years after its birth, when the art was already full grown. Three million telephones stood abroad, he notes, and seven million in America, the land of its birth. The book tells how ridicule gave way to wonder, and how the phone remade business and home.

Casson follows Bell and his rivals, the growth of exchanges, and the spread of wires across cities and farms. His prose is brisk and popular, full of anecdotes of first calls and early mishaps. The book is a vivid snapshot of a new technology in its first triumph, written while the wonder was still fresh.
860-baby-mine:
Margaret Mayo wrote this domestic comedy about Alfred Hardy, a young man of fixed ideas and high ideals, proud of both. His college friend Jimmy Jinks, who has few ideas and no ideals, is glad of it, and the contrast between the two men drives the fun. Marriage, pride, and a baby soon test Alfred's fine theories.

Mayo writes with warmth and pace, turning a household tangle into farce without losing sympathy for her people. The comedy made her name on stage and in print, and its situations still ring true. The book suits readers who enjoy a light, well-made comedy about love, pride, and the gap between ideals and life.
a-florentine-tragedy-la-sainte-courtisan:
Oscar Wilde left both of these verse plays unfinished, and they appear here in a 1917 Methuen volume of his miscellaneous works, with a preface explaining their history. A Florentine Tragedy is set in Renaissance Florence, where a merchant comes home to find his wife with a young noble. La Sainte Courtisane turns to the Egyptian desert, a holy hermit, and a beautiful courtesan.

In Florence, talk of cloth and money turns to swords before the night ends. In the desert piece, the hermit and the courtesan trade faith and desire in rich, strange speeches. Both fragments show Wilde reaching beyond drawing-room comedy toward dark, poetic drama, and both break off before completion.
a-rebellious-heroine:
John Kendrick Bangs plays a literary game in this tale from the 1896 Harper and Brothers edition, illustrated by W. T. Smedley. A novelist finds that the heroine he invented will not stay inside the story he planned for her. She has opinions about her own plot, her hero, and her author, and she acts on them.

The comedy runs on the collision between the author's intentions and his character's free will, a joke Bangs handles with the light touch of his House-Boat on the Styx. Chapters move between the writing desk and the world of the book. The piece is an early, cheerful example of fiction laughing at its own machinery.
a-ride-across-palestine:
Anthony Trollope tells how circumstances took him to the Holy Land without a companion, in this tale from the 1864 Tales of All Countries. He calls himself a gregarious animal, meant to go in pairs, and owns he was sad at heart in his Jerusalem hotel. Next morning he starts on horseback for the Dead Sea, Jordan, and Jericho.

Alone among strangers, he falls in with a fellow traveler whose company changes the ride, and the tale turns from sightseeing to character. Church of the Sepulchre, Mount of Olives, and Bethany pass by, but Trollope's interest is the living people on the road. The piece is travel writing worn as fiction, in his easy, confiding voice.
alone:
Norman Douglas wrote Alone as a book of travel sketches, most of them Italian, and dedicated it to his friend Edward Hutton. The contents run from Mentone and Levanto to Siena, Pisa, Viareggio, Rome, Olevano. Sorrento, with an introduction that looks back at the Great War and his comic failure to find patriotic employment in London offices.

Each place gets a loose essay of walks, inns, food, talk, and people met by the way, written in Douglas's dry, amused voice. Nothing is systematic: a town is a starting point for memory, argument, and appetite. Readers who know South Wind, named on his title page, will recognize the manner — a cultivated idler thinking aloud in Mediterranean sun.
anomalies-and-curiosities-of-medicine:
George M. Gould and Walter L. Pyle compiled this encyclopedic collection of medical anomalies. Its title page announces the scope: rare and extraordinary cases, and the most striking instances of abnormality in all branches of medicine and surgery. The material is drawn from medical literature from its origin to the present day, then abstracted, classified, annotated, and indexed.

The introductory essay argues that the anomalous has always driven science: monsters and strange growths show nature's workshop with its guard down. The body of the book then catalogs case after case from journals and older authors — unusual births, giant and dwarf growth, strange injuries survived, foreign bodies, and odd diseases. It became a standard sourcebook for physicians and, later, for writers of medical curiosities, valued for its citations as much as its wonders.
baby-mine:
Margaret Mayo built her farce Baby Mine around Alfred Hardy, a young husband of fixed ideas who wants children. His college friend Jimmy Jinks happily lets Alfred make up his mind for him. Alfred's wife Zoie has other plans, and deception begins. The novel follows the hit stage play Mayo also wrote.

Zoie and her friend Aggie borrow babies to sustain a lie. The borrowed infants multiply until husbands find themselves holding three youngsters at once. Smashed glass, whispered warnings, and doors closed softly mark the escalating panic. Mayo keeps the machinery brisk and the dialogue rapid. The comedy was a Broadway success, and its situation, a wife's fib meeting a husband's obsession, still plays cleanly.
beechcroft-at-rockstone:
Charlotte M. Yonge's Beechcroft at Rockstone opens with a telegram in the Mohun sisters' parlour. Jane Mohun reads it: Lily, Jasper, accident, come. Her delicate sister Adeline stipulates conditions from her chair. Jane packs her ever-ready bag and catches the 11.20 train.

Sir Jasper's accident disperses his children among relations, and Beechcroft takes its share of the household. Gillian's help, the Halfpenny mother, and little Primrose arrive in Jane's planning. Rockstone is the family's seaside place, where invalids and schoolgirls must be fitted into a small house. Yonge's dispersion becomes an education: duty distributed among the willing and the reluctant. The novel belongs to her Mohun family chronicle. Its pleasures are small, exact, and moral, the management of a household standing in for the government of a soul.
betty-zane:
Zane Grey's first novel, Betty Zane, honors his own ancestor, Elizabeth Zane. Her heroism came at the siege of Fort Henry in 1782. His author's note calls that fight the last battle of the American Revolution. Grey dedicates the book to the Betty Zane chapter of the Daughters of the Revolution and doubts the magazine versions he had read. Colonel Ebenezer Zane's frontier settlement at Wheeling anchors the story.

Betty runs powder through enemy fire to save the fort. The hunter Lewis Wetzel moves through the woods chapters like a force of nature. Betty herself must hold his knife arm when he rises against an enemy. Grey built a career on this mixture of family legend, frontier history, and romance.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-dunf: The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Dunfermline describes a Scottish abbey founded about 1070 by King Malcolm Canmore and Queen Margaret. David the First remodelled it as a Benedictine house with an abbot and twelve monks from Canterbury. Its buildings were so vast that three sovereigns with their retinues might lodge there together, though Edward the First burned them in 1304. Dunfermline took Iona's place as Scotland's royal burial ground, the Westminster Abbey of Scotland, holding Malcolm, Margaret, David the First and Robert Bruce. Its tombs survive within the ruined Lady chapel.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-sain: The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on St. Augustine's describes a Benedictine monastery at Canterbury, founded in 605 on the site of St. Pancras' church. King Ethelbert had given that church to St. Augustine in 597. Named for Sts. Peter and Paul, it was enlarged and renamed in 978 by St. Dunstan for Peter, Paul and Augustine, whose body lay in the crypt. At the dissolution in 1538 the abbot and thirty monks gave it up for pensions. Henry the Eighth took it as a palace, and in 1844 its remains were sold for a college.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-acacius-bisho:
Acacius, Bishop of Caesarea in Palestine, was disciple and biographer of Eusebius the historian, succeeding him in the see in 340. Nothing is known of his birth date or country, though he was probably a Syrian. His nickname, monophthalmos, one-eyed, likely came from a personal defect, though possibly also as a sly comment on his shiftiness and his rare gift for ambiguous statement.

He was a deeply learned prelate and a patron of studies, author of a treatise on Ecclesiastes and of six books of miscellanies surviving only in fragments. He is chiefly remembered for opposing St. Cyril of Jerusalem bitterly and for his shifting part in the Arian controversy. He professed the Nicaean formularies under Jovian in 363, swung back under Valens in 364, was condemned at Lampsacus, and, Baronius says, died in 366.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-adam-of-perse:
Adam of Perseigne was a French Cistercian, Abbot of Perseigne in the diocese of Mans, born about the middle of the twelfth century. Thought first a canon regular, later a Marmoutier Benedictine, then a Cistercian. About 1180 he became Abbot of Perseigne, where his holy, wise reputation drew leading figures of his time for counsel.

At Rome he conferred with Calabria's celebrated mystic Joachim, Abbot of Flora, on the latter's revelations, and he helped Foulques de Neuilly preach the Fourth Crusade. Rome published his letters and sermons in 1662 under the title Adami Abbatis Perseniae Ordinis Cisterciensis Mariale. The entry cites Mignon in the dictionary of Catholic theology for this brief monastic life.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alphonse-de-l:
Alphonse de Lamartine, French poet, was born at Mâcon in 1790, died at Paris in 1869. Born of a noble Christian family, he read the Bible. Later he read Fénelon, Bernardin de Saint-Pierre, Chateaubriand, Mme de Staël, Racine, Voltaire, Parny, Tasso, Dante, Petrarch, Shakespeare, Ossian, especially the last. About twenty, he met Graziella, a cigarette girl, at a relative's house in Naples.

Hitherto an imitator, henceforth his guide was his own inspiration. Madame Charles is his Raphael's Julie and his poems' Elvire. He entered poetry with Les Méditations Poétiques of 1820, awaking famous. Other works: Les Secondes Méditations (1823), Harmonies Poétiques et Religieuses (1830), Jocelyn (1836), La Chute d'un Ange (1838). Two epic fragments dreamed for humanity and Recueillements Poétiques (1839) returned to lyricism, below his early works. In 1835 he published Voyage en Orient, a brilliant account of his Orient journey, losing his daughter. Thenceforth he wrote prose only.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alsace-lorrai:
Alsace-Lorraine is the German Imperial Territory so known, divided for state purposes into three civil districts. Lower and Upper Alsace and Lorraine include the bishoprics of Strasbourg and Metz, immediately subject to the Holy See. The census of 1 December 1900 distributes the population as follows. Strasbourg diocese: 821,612 Catholics, 304,204 Protestants, 3,192 Dissidents, 25,414 Jews, 319 of unknown religion, 1,154,741 total. Metz diocese: 488,838 Catholics, 67,874 Protestants, 1,224 Dissidents, 6,850 Jews, 43 of unknown religion, 564,829 total.

These figures exclude 34,367 Strasbourg soldiers and 44,491 Metz soldiers, under the Army Bishop in Berlin's jurisdiction. The entry treats cathedral chapters, diocesan administration, parishes, stipends, church taxes, and religious houses. It also covers clerical seminaries, episcopal gymnasia, collections among the faithful, elementary education, art monuments, and institutions of charity. The Bishop of Strasbourg has made six church collections obligatory. They fall on the Sunday after Epiphany for the African missions, on Good Friday for the Christians of the East, and at Easter and Pentecost.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-altar-stone:
The altar stone is one solid piece of natural stone, blessed by a bishop, big enough for Sacred Host and chalice. The stone must be natural and solid, not some other material at all. It is set into or placed on a structure serving as an altar where the whole altar is unconsecrated. Sometimes the whole table, or mensa, replaces the smaller stone.

Called a portable altar, it lets Mass be said where no consecrated altar stands. Its consecration by a bishop gives even a makeshift altar its sacred character.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-altar-wine:
Altar wine is one of the two elements required for the Eucharist, pure grape juice naturally and properly fermented, called vinum de vite. Raisin wine may serve if colour and taste judge it pure, and it comes sweet or dry, weak or strong, white or red. Since only genuine wine makes the sacrifice valid and licit, the celebrant must procure pure wines. Safest is buying directly from a conscientious manufacturer rather than second hand.

Vinegar, putrid or corrupted wine, unripe-grape pressings, and wine so watered it can hardly be called wine are forbidden. Wine turning to vinegar or putrid, and unfermented juice, are grievous matter to use yet still valid. Weak wines may be conserved with a little grape brandy or alcohol against souring in transport, under stated conditions.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ambrogio-borg:
Ambrogio Borgognone, real name Ambrogio Stefani da Fossano, was a distinguished Italian painter and architect, born at Milan about 1455 and dead there in 1523. His name's origin is variously explained. He painted in tempera, in oil in tempera's style, and in fresco; early work lacked freedom, but Leonardo da Vinci's beneficent influence later shaped him.

The Certosa near Pavia's façade is credited to him, its choir stalls and woodwork carved from his designs, with his Crucifixion altarpiece painted there. Great refinement and deep religious feeling shape his work, with beautiful celestial and mundane types. Public galleries hold his Marriage of St. Catherine at London's National Gallery and Madonna pictures at Berlin, Munich, and Dresden. Milan's Brera holds the Assumption, and Pavia Academy holds Christ Bearing His Cross.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ancient-dioce:
Lindisfarne, now called Holy Island, lies about two miles off the Northumberland coast, south-east of Berwick. About three miles long and one and a half wide, it joins the mainland at low water. A three-mile track from Beal crosses the sands, marked by wooden posts. Saint Aidan, a Columban monk-bishop from Iona, founded his see here in 635 at King Oswald's request.

The island became the mother church of Northumbria, seat of sixteen bishops and a centre of missionary work. It earned the name Iona of England. Bishop Carileph gave Lindisfarne to the Benedictines of Durham in 1082. Its Norman church rose under them, and the priory lived until 1536. The site passed to the Dean and Chapter of Durham, then to the crown in 1613. Its famous gospel codex, lost for a century, reached the British Museum by way of Sir Robert Cotton.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-andrea-ciccio:
Doubt surrounds Andrea Ciccione, a sculptor and architect born at Naples in the early fifteenth century. Writers of note omit him entirely, while others, found reliable, record him. A pupil of Masuccio the younger, he is said to have built San Severino's cloister, the church and monastery of Monte Oliveto, and several palaces.

He carved the monument of Giosue Caracciolo. Queen Joanna II picked him to make the tomb of her brother King Ladislaus in San Giovanni a Carbonara. It towers three stories, flanked by allegorical figures, with Ladislaus on his war horse at the top. Joanna hired him again after her lover Gian Caracciolo was murdered. Above that tomb stands a sarcophagus carried by three armed knights for Justice, Strength, and Prudence. Caracciolo stands above, coloured as if alive. The tombs draw notice for colour work and virtues dressed as soldiers. No dates survive for Ciccione.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-andrew-byrne:
Andrew Byrne, Bishop of Little Rock, was born at Navan in Ireland in 1802 and died at Helena, Arkansas, in 1862. A student when Bishop England sought volunteers in 1820 for the new Diocese of Charleston, he accompanied the bishop to the United States. Ordained at Charleston in 1827, he did missionary work in the Carolinas and served years as vicar-general.

In 1836 he moved to New York, serving at Saint Patrick's, Saint James's, and the Nativity. In 1843 he turned Carroll Hall, cradle of New York's school system, into Saint Andrew's church. While pastor in 1844, the Diocese of Little Rock was created, and Byrne was named its bishop. Arkansas then held only about 700 Catholics with one priest and two churches. Before his death he claimed nine priests, eleven churches, thirty stations, and twelve schools. He visited Ireland for workers, introduced the Sisters of Mercy from Dublin, and nearly arranged a Fort Smith college.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antiochus-of-:
Antiochus of Palestine, seventh-century monk born near Ancyra, lived first solitary, then became Abbot of St. Saba's laura near Jerusalem. He witnessed the 614 Persian invasion and Bedouin massacre of forty-four companions. After Chosroes conquered the Holy Land, Ancyra fell in 619, forcing Attaline's monks to wander homeless. Unable to carry many books, they had Eustathius ask Antiochus for a Scripture abridgment and martyrdom account.

In compliance he wrote the Pandects of Holy Scripture, 130 chapters of moral sentences drawn from Scripture and early ecclesiastical writers. He also wrote an Exomologesis prayer relating Jerusalem's miseries since the Persian invasion and begging divine mercy for the Holy City. The Pandects' first chapter tells the martyrdom; its last lists heretics from Simon Magus to Severus of Antioch's Monophysite followers. The book is specially valuable for extracts of lost works, showing an then-uncommon interest in early Christian literature.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antoine-elisa:
Antoine-Elisabeth Dareste de la Chavanne, a French historian born in Paris in 1820, taught history for decades at Lyons. After study at the Ecole Normale, he took a doctorate in letters. He held chairs at Grenoble and then at Lyons, where he served twenty years and became dean of letters in 1865. Several of his books won prizes from the French Academy.

His works ranged from a study of French administration since Philip Augustus to a history of farming classes. His largest work was an eight-volume history of France. Written clearly and fully, they treated the Roman Church fairly despite his Gallican leanings, a French view that stressed local church rights. Late in life he helped found the Catholic University of Lyons and served as rector of its academy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-assistant-at-:
Assistants at the Pontifical Throne, in Latin assistens throno pontificio, are bishops belonging to the Papal Chapel who stand toward the pope much as cathedral canons stand toward their bishop. At solemn functions these assistants, wearing cope and mitre, surround the pope's throne, while other bishops lack privilege to stand in his immediate vicinity.

To this college belong ex officio certain archbishops and bishops, plus those to whom the pope has given the privilege by brief, or short papal letter. Throne assistants rank immediately after cardinals, may celebrate Mass in private oratories, and may dispose of a set sum from their episcopal benefices for clerics or relations. They may also set it aside for their own obsequies. They are always made counts of the Apostolic Palace and belong to the Pontifical Family.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-asylums-and-c:
Asylums and Care for the Insane argues against a common reproach. That reproach says proper care for the insane and fitting institutions arose only in recent generations, and that the church, so active in humanitarian work, failed here. During the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries hospital treatment and nursing fell to their lowest ebb in history, and care for the insane shared that decay and was its worst feature.

As a matter of fact, the article argues, the church from earliest times arranged care for the insane, and some arrangements anticipated important modern advances. It was following the religious revolt in Germany, felt in other countries, that church charitable institutions suffered and hospitals and asylums of all kinds declined. Insanity has been known as long as recorded history runs, and the entry follows care from early church provision through Pinel and modern reform.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-augusta-theod:
Augusta Theodosia Drane, known in religion as Mother Francis Raphael, was an English Dominican writer born near London in 1823 who died at Stone in 1894. Her parents were Protestants, and her father managed an East India trading house. Wide reading in youth fed her gifts, and Burnet's History of the Reformation, she said, first caused her conversion. She consulted Keble and Pusey without satisfaction, but a local vicar's talk of the Third Order of St Dominic moved her deeply.

She was received into the Church at Tiverton in 1850 and entered the Dominican Third Order at Clifton in 1852. At Stone she taught, wrote, and rose through office: mistress of novices, mistress of studies, prioress, and finally provincial in 1881. Her books ranged from lives of St Dominic and St Catherine of Siena to histories of England, tales, and school texts. She also translated Lacordaire's Inner Life and edited the papers of Archbishop Ullathorne.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-baldassare-ca:
Baldassare Castiglione was an Italian prose writer born near Mantua in 1478, who died at Toledo in 1529. After classical schooling at Milan, he served Ludovico il Moro, then Francesco Gonzaga of Mantua. In 1504 Urbino became his home, in service to Duke Guidobaldo da Montefeltro, where he spent his best years. That court's splendor drew the age's finest writers and artists.

In 1513 Guidobaldo's heir made him a count and later ambassador to the Holy See. Pope Clement VII sent him as envoy to Charles V in 1524, but Rome was sacked in 1527 and Clement captured. The disaster broke Castiglione in health and spirits and hastened his death. His fame rests on the Cortegiano, in four books, picturing the ideal courtier's accomplishments and character. Begun in 1514 and finished four years later, it waited until 1528 for print and reached a dozen languages.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bayonne:
Bayonne, ancient Lapurdum, is a diocese covering the Basses-Pyrénées, reorganized in 1802 to absorb Oloron, Lescar, and parishes of Dax and Tarbes. Suffragan to Toulouse until 1822, it then passed to Auch. Tradition names the martyr St Leo, of the miraculous fountain, its first bishop, but no bishop is historically known before the sixth century. Until 1655 it held Spanish lands, four archpresbyteries left from Charlemagne's conquests beyond the Pyrenees.

Lescar's legend claims St Julian as first bishop, but history names Galactorius of Lescar and Gratus of Oloron, both at Agde in 506. Christopher de Beaumont, later Archbishop of Paris, held Bayonne from 1741 to 1745, and Astros from 1820 to 1830. Betharram's Auxiliary Priests of the Sacred Heart, founded in 1841, teach and mission from Bethlehem to Buenos Aires and Montevideo. The Bernardines of Anglet, founded in 1846, keep perpetual silence between prayer and needlework.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bernard-of-bo:
Bernard of Botone, generally called Parmensis after Parma, his birthplace, was a noted thirteenth-century canonist, profiled in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia. His birth date is unknown, and he died in 1263, or by another account in 1266. Under Tancred he studied canon law at Bologna, where he later held the chair and taught Durantis.

A canonry at Bologna cathedral and chaplaincies to Popes Innocent IV and Alexander IV placed him at the centre of church law. His glosses, or line-by-line notes, on the Decretals became a standard teaching text. His tomb inscription calls him chancellor of the University of Bologna, a fitting honour for a master of the schools.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-berne:
Berne, the Swiss federal capital since 1848, receives a full entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia. Fourth city of Switzerland in population and capital of its canton, it stands nearly 1,800 feet above sea level on a peninsula thrust into the River Aar. Its people grew from about 5,000 in the Middle Ages to 64,064 in 1900, mostly German-speaking Protestants.

Bridges, churches, and civic buildings fill the middle of the piece, from the iron Kirchenfeld bridge to the Holy Trinity church and the parliament buildings of 1895 to 1902. Catholic life, a minority of about 6,278 souls, gets its own count of parishes and schools. The entry joins topography, history, and church statistics in one civic portrait.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bl-john-payne:
Blessed John Payne, a martyr, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born in the Diocese of Peterborough, he died at Chelmsford on 2 April 1582. He reached Douai in 1574 and took orders at Cambrai two years later, and sailed for England with Blessed Cuthbert Mayne, living mostly with Anne Petre at Ingatestone in Essex.

Early in July 1581 he and George Godsalve were arrested in Warwickshire through the spy Eliot, examined by Walsingham, and sent to the Tower, where Payne was racked twice. Eliot charged him with a plot against the queen's life, and though no proof backed the tale, a Chelmsford jury gave the expected verdict. At his execution the crowd stopped the final barbarities until he was dead.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bl-john-stone: Blessed John Stone, an English martyr, was executed at the Dane-John in Canterbury, likely in December 1539, for rejecting the king's supremacy. An Austin friar of Canterbury and doctor of divinity, he was the friar of whom Bishop Ingworth complained in December 1538. Ingworth said Stone held at all times that the king may not head the Church of England. In prison, after three days of fasting, he heard a voice urging courage for the truth.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-blessed-delph: Blessed Delphine, a member of the Franciscan Third Order, was born in Provence in 1284 and died on 26 November 1358. Orphaned in infancy, she was raised under her uncles' guardianship and her aunt, Abbess of St. Catherine of Sorbo. She took a vow of virginity and kept it faithfully. Married at twenty to Elzéar, Count of Sarban, the couple took the Third Order habit and lived in prayer, penance, and charity until his death in 1323.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-blessed-marga:
Margaret of Lorraine, Duchess of Alencon, turned from court life to found a Poor Clare monastery at Argentan. Born at Vaudemont in 1463 and orphaned young, she was raised by her grandfather Rene of Anjou. She married the Duke of Alencon in 1488 and was widowed in 1492.

After ruling her duchy and raising her children, she retired to Mortagne with sisters following the rule of Saint Elizabeth. She then brought nuns to Argentan and placed the new house under Saint Clare's rule. She took the habit there and made vows in October 1520. She died a year later at sixty-two. Efforts to gain Roman recognition of her cult were still under way when the entry was written.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bodone:
Bodone, a titular see of Albania, stands on the site of ancient Dodona in Epirus, below Mount Tomaros near Janina. A Christian church rose there on the temple of Zeus. Bishops of Dodona appear at Ephesus in 431, Chalcedon in 451, and in letters to Emperor Leo in 458 and Pope Hormisdas in 516.

When Naupactus replaced Nicopolis late in the tenth century, Dodona became its first suffragan see. Later lists call it Bounditza or Bonditza, and John of Bonditza signed a synodal act in 1229. The Greek residential bishopric vanished at an unknown date. Rome long used the forms Bodona and Bodonensis, and an 1894 decree ordered the see suppressed at its titular's death.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-brisbane:
Brisbane, the Queensland diocese south of the 24th parallel, covers some 200,000 square miles with its cathedral city as state capital. Settled as a convict station in 1825 and opened to free settlers in 1842, the Moreton Bay District held only 2,257 white souls in 1843, with one shanty church and no school. Passionists tried an aboriginal mission on Stradbroke Island in 1843 and left by 1846.

Fathers McGinnety and Hanly arrived in December 1843 as the first stationed priests, and the diocese rose in 1859 with James O'Quinn as first bishop. He found two priests, two churches, two schools, and 7,676 Catholics in a vast see. Arriving with five priests and six sisters in 1861, he organized immigration, endured bare-earth beds and damper fare on visitations, and built the church across Queensland.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-caltagirone:
Caltagirone is a Sicilian city in the province of Catania, built on two heights about 2,000 feet above the sea and joined by a bridge. Some take it for ancient Hybla Minor, others for ancient Gela. In the Middle Ages Saracens made it a stronghold, and its name's first syllables come from the Arabic kalaat, castle. Genoese failed to drive the Arabs out, but the Normans later took it with the rest of Sicily.

It once belonged to Syracuse, and when Syracuse became a metropolis, Caltagirone rose as its suffragan, its first bishop being Gaetano Maria Trigona, later moved to Palermo. The diocese counts 115,500 people, with 25 parishes, 112 churches and chapels, and 199 secular and 48 regular priests.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-carcassonne:
Carcassonne is a French diocese covering the whole department of Aude as suffragan to Toulouse. The Concordat of 1802 joined several older sees into one. The old diocese of Carcassonne, nearly all of Narbonne, most of Saint-Papoul, parts of Alet and Mirepoix, plus the old Perpignan diocese formed the new see. Perpignan was restored as its own diocese in 1822.

The diocese itself dates from after 533, when Visigoths sought a bishopric to offset losing Lodève and Uzès, with Sergius in 589 as its first known bishop. The entry also traces Narbonne, whose first bishop Paulus is linked by local tradition to Sergius Paulus of the Acts. Later holders include Guy Goulques, who became Pope Clement IV, and Bishop de la Bouillerie, a mystical writer, at Carcassonne from 1855 to 1873.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-carlo-vercell:
Carlo Vercellone was a Barnabite biblical scholar born at Biella who died at Rome in January 1869. He joined the order at Genoa in 1829. He read philosophy in Turin and theology in Rome under Aloysius Ungarelli, and taught sacred subjects in Alessandria, Turin, Perugia, and Parma. In 1847 he became president of the Barnabite college at Rome, later adding the offices of procurator and then general of his order.

His first publication, in 1857, was a five-volume edition of the Vatican manuscript of Scripture prepared by Cardinal Mai. Its preface letter admitted its flaws. He at once set out to correct it from Mai's notes, producing a new octavo New Testament at Rome in 1859. Later work defended the authenticity of the adulteress passage in John's Gospel. He edited nine Gerdil pamphlets on church hierarchy and answered Renan on Semitic languages in 1869.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cavaliere-par:
Paris Bordone was an eminent painter of the Venetian school, born at Treviso in 1500 and dying at Venice in 1570. Of noble family, he entered Titian's school and studied there for several years. Afterwards he learned from Giorgione. Feeling the influence of both, he settled into Titian's manner so well that his paintings are at times taken for Titian's own.

In portraiture he yielded to none but Titian. Early work took him to Venice, Vicenza, and Treviso. At Treviso his dome paintings at San Vicenzo showed the Annunciation, Nativity, Adoration of the Shepherds, Crucifixion, Ascension, and Assumption. Invited to France, where he was knighted, he painted the royal family and court figures before returning to Italy, leaving works in Venice, Rome, Padua, and Genoa.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cesar-guillau:
César Guillaume La Luzerne was a French cardinal born at Paris in 1738 and dying there in 1821. Educated at the Collège de Navarre, he rose through his kinsmen the Lamoignons to the See of Langres in 1770, which made him duke and peer of the realm. He then sat in the Assembly of Notables in 1788 and the Estates-General in 1789.

His efforts to hold the Constituent Assembly to moderation failed, and he withdrew from it. In 1791 he refused the constitutional oath and left for Constance and Venice, where he housed French exiles generously and wrote at length. After the Restoration he returned, became cardinal and state minister in 1817, and regained Langres. An able apologist, he stood for an old Gallicanism whose revival failed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-chalons-sur-m:
Châlons-sur-Marne is a diocese comprising the department of Marne, except for the arrondissement of Reims. Joined to Meaux in 1802 and to Reims in 1821, it was re-established in 1822 as suffragan to Reims. Local legends credit St. Memmius, sent by St. Peter with his sister Poma and Sts. Donatian and Domitian, with evangelizing Châlons in the first century, but the revised Breviary list of diocesan saints suppresses these legends.

Abbé Duchesne dates the see's founding to the fourth century. Amandinus, its ninth bishop, attended the Council of Tours in 461. St. Lumier, bishop about 580, was famed for miraculous power over animals. At Capetian coronations the Châlons bishop invariably bore the royal ring. Eugene III consecrated the cathedral in 1147, assisted by St. Bernard and eighteen cardinals. At the close of 1905 the diocese counted 231,411 people.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charlemagne:
Charlemagne, Charles the Great, was king of the Franks and the West's first Christian emperor. He was born in 742 and died at Aachen in 814. His birthplace, Aachen or Liège, was never settled. Son of Pepin the Short, he won Rome's acknowledgment as its chief protector. Of fifty-three campaigns, only a dozen or so were not fought for the Church. Eighteen campaigns against the Saxons sought to extinguish their pagan worship.

In his later years his sons led expeditions such as Louis's capture of Barcelona. He worked to conciliate jealous Constantinople, which treated the Roman crowning as schism. He stayed healthy until his sixty-eighth year, when fevers struck and left him limping. He acted as his own physician, resisting doctors who urged boiled meat over roast. No portrait from his lifetime survives, though a very ancient statuette stands in the Musée Carnavalet at Paris.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-erski:
Charles Erskine was a cardinal born at Rome in 1739 and dead at Paris in 1811. Son of Colin Erskine and Agatha Gigli of Anagni, he was educated by Cardinal Henry, Duke of York, at the Scots College in Rome. In 1782 Pius VI gave him the pro-auditorship and the Promoter of the Faith office, then domestic prelacy, a St. Peter's canonry, and the deanship of the consistorial advocates.

Sent as papal envoy to England in October 1793, Erskine built excellent relations with court and ministry. He left in 1801, returned to Rome, and was created cardinal in January 1803. After the French invasion of 1808 he shared the pope's confinement in the Quirinal. Napoleon ordered him to Paris in 1809, and ill health forced the journey in January 1810; he declined gradually and died there.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-farra:
Charles Farrar Browne, known as Artemus Ward, was a humorist born at Waterford, Maine, in 1834 and dead at Southampton, England, in 1867. Schooled in his native town, he entered the Skowhegan Clarion printing office as an apprentice at fourteen. A year later he worked in Boston on the Carpet-Bag.

In 1858, at twenty-four, his national reputation began as a reporter for the Cleveland Plaindealer under the name Artemus Ward. He later edited a paper in the manner of London's Punch, succeeding Charles G. Leland. Yet it was as a lecturer that he won fame and fortune, from Babes in the Woods in New York to Sixty Minutes in Africa in Philadelphia. In 1866 he sailed for England, where London hailed him and his Punch letters recalled Yellowplush, before sickness cut his brilliant career short.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-marie:
An entry on Charles Marie de La Condamine, the French explorer and physicist who measured the shape of the earth in South America. Born in Paris in 1701, he served briefly as a soldier, then explored African and Asia Minor coasts before being chosen in 1735 to lead an expedition to the equator. Its task was to measure a meridian, a north-south arc, and so settle whether the globe flattens toward the poles.

With companions Bouguer and Godin, and Spanish officers Juan and Ulloa, La Condamine worked eight years in Ecuador, triangulating mountain country and noting that tall peaks deflect a pendulum by their pull. The expedition opened tropical America to wider science, though its instruments were crude by later standards. He is also credited with bringing rubber, called caoutchouc, into Europe and with trying to introduce smallpox inoculation in France. He died in Paris in 1774.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cheyenne:
Wyoming, an area of 97,575 square miles, forms the Diocese of Cheyenne. Founded on 9 August 1887, it had been part of the Diocese of Omaha and before that of the Vicariate of Nebraska. Its first bishop, Maurice Burke, was consecrated in October 1887. The first recorded Mass in Wyoming was said by the Jesuit Father De Smet on Green River's open prairie on 4 July 1840.

De Smet passed through Wyoming many times as missionary and army chaplain, and Canadian priests ministered at Fort Laramie. Settlement was slow on the arid soil, railroads came late, and many Catholics lived thirty years without Mass or priest. By the census of 1907 the diocese counted about 10,000 Catholics in a population of 100,000, with twenty-two churches, seventeen priests, twenty missions without churches, and St. Stephen's Mission Indian school.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-christian-doc:
A vast entry on Christian doctrine, taken first as the act of teaching and the knowledge taught, the same as catechesis and catechism. Didaskalia and didache in the New Testament, doctrina in the Vulgate, mark teaching as a bishop's chief duty in the Pastoral Epistles. Katechesis means instruction by word of mouth, above all by question and answer, for those preparing to enter Christianity.

The entry treats its subject under three heads: history of catechetics, practical catechetics, and modern catechisms. Oral question-and-answer teaching held a leading place in the moral and religious schools of the Church. The word catechism once meant the act of teaching itself, as Shakespeare uses it, and only later settled on the printed question-and-answer book. Its history runs from apostolic instruction through medieval and modern schools to the catechisms of the present day.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cloyne:
Cloyne, from Gaelic Cluain-uania, Cave-meadow, covers the northern half of County Cork. It counts 140 priests, 47 parishes, 16 convents, 8 Brothers' schools, 235 primary schools, Saint Colman's College, and Loreto Convent at Fermoy, besides high schools at Queenstown, now Cobh, and elsewhere. Saint Colman's Cathedral at Queenstown, begun in 1869 under Bishop Keane and continued under Bishop McCarthy, stood near completion in 1908. The medieval cathedral still stands at Cloyne, used by Protestants since the sixteenth century.

Saint Colman MacLenin, from 560 to 601, turned from poet-historian to become first Bishop of Cloyne in 560, receiving a royal land grant. Religious poems are attributed to him, including a life of Saint Senan. Fergal, Abbot-Bishop of Cloyne, was massacred by Danes in 888, and Cloyne suffered seven devastations from 822 to 1137. Church records were destroyed, so few prelates before 1137 are known. In 1152 the Synod of Kells made Cloyne one of Cashel's twelve suffragan sees.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cologne:
Joseph Lins's entry covers Cologne as both a German city and an archbishopric. The city, third in Prussia, lies on both banks of the lower Rhine. It covered 45 square miles. On 1 December 1905 it held 428,722 people, of whom 339,790 were Catholics. Its history runs back before Christ. After Agrippa moved the Ubii across the Rhine in 38 B.C., their center stood on the site. In A.D. 50 Agrippina founded the colony of veterans called Colonia Agrippina.

Cologne grew rich in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries. In the sixteenth-century religious upheavals it stayed Catholic, thanks largely to its university. Its cathedral stands as the greatest Gothic monument in Germany. The archbishopric, first surely held by Saint Maternus in 314, later made its holders princes of the Empire. Five Wittelsbach electors ruled it to 1761, and in 1750 it counted 860 parishes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-compline:
Fernand Cabrol's entry explains Compline, from the Latin completorium, a complement. It closes the day's Hours, completing them all. Saint Benedict first used the word in this sense near the start of the sixth century, in chapters of his Rule. He even used the verb complere for the Hour itself. In the Roman Breviary, Compline falls into parts: introduction, psalmody with anthems, hymn, capitulum, response, evangelical canticle, prayer, and benediction. The shape is spare, fit for night's edge.

Its origin has lately stirred much debate among liturgists. General opinion, Cabrol notes, traces the Hour through early monastic practice, with Eastern monks before Chalcedon as witnesses. Sources run from Pargoire and Besse to Bishop's study of a seventh-century service book and Cabrol's own book on ancient prayer. The entry thus gives a short Hour a long pedigree, from Benedict's Rule to modern discussion of its roots.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-confraternity:
Michael Glancey's entry follows the Confraternity of Christian Doctrine, founded at Rome in 1562 to give religious instruction. To about the thirteenth century, Creed and Paternoster formed instruction's base, learned by heart and explained by parish priests on Sundays and feasts. Then Commandments, sacraments, virtues, and vices widened the range. Lambeth's synod of 1281, under Archbishop Peckham, asked priests to explain faith's truths four times yearly. Lavaur's provincial council of 1368 ordered teaching every Sunday and feast day, publishing a catechism for Languedoc and Gascony clergy.

Organized instruction had already begun before 1562. Westminster's First Provincial Council urged the confraternity's members for Sunday and day schools, though Sunday schools abound while the confraternity lags. Kindred bodies include Brussels' Pieuses Unions of 1851 and the Paris Voluntary Catechists, aiding priests with laicized primary schools. Leo XIII raised that work to archconfraternity rank in 1893, with power to affiliate French sisters. Indulgences for these groups run very numerous.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-corner-stone:
Herbert Thurston's entry treats the corner stone, or foundation stone. The Roman Pontifical provides a rite, De benedictione et impositione Primarii Lapidis, for blessing and laying a church's foundation stone. Appearing in the same form in the Giunta Pontificale of 1520, the rite probably dates at least from Patricius Piccolomini's fifteenth century. It may in substance reach two centuries further back, to Durandus of Mende.

Before building begins, the rubric directs provision for the church's maintenance, foundations marked out with the bishop's or his delegate's approval, and a wooden cross where the altar will stand. In the ensuing function the bishop first blesses the stone. Medieval practice knew this or some analogous rite, though few Pontificals contain anything of the sort. Assigning a date to the blessing practice's beginning proves difficult. Questions arise over laying money on the stone for the fabric, and enclosing coins within or beneath it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cotrone:
Cotrone, a suffragan diocese of Reggio on Calabria's Ionian coast, stands on ancient Croton, an Achaean colony founded about 707 BC. Croton flourished in Magna Graecia, famed for strong, sober citizens, for Milo the athlete, and for Pythagoras, who founded his school there. Conquerors from Dionysius to Hannibal seized it in turn.

Local legend credits St Dionysius the Areopagite with preaching the Gospel there, and Flavianus stands as its first known bishop. Later bishops include Minturno the polished writer, the Dominican Juan Lopez, and Niceforo Melisseno Commeno, who served the Holy See abroad. The diocese counts 14,000 souls, ten parishes, and twenty-nine churches and chapels.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-count-carlo-o:
A biographical entry introduces Count Carlo Ottavio Castiglione, a Milanese philologist and numismatist, meaning a scholar of languages and of coins, born in 1784 and dead in 1849. Descended from Baldassare Castiglione, author of The Courtier, he mastered almost all the Indo-Germanic and Semitic languages while still young.

His published work ranged from a description of Cufic, or early Arabic-script, coins in Milan's Brera collection to a geographical and numismatic memoir on eastern Barbary and the Atlantic Berbers. Outside Italy he is best known for editing fragments of the Gothic Bible translation by Ulfilas, found among palimpsests, reused manuscripts, in the Ambrosian Library. He also left many unpublished writings on language.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cuthbert-mayn:
A biographical entry tells of Cuthbert Mayne, martyr, baptized near Barnstaple in March 1544 and executed at Launceston on 29 November 1577. Son of William Mayne, he was schooled by a schismatical uncle, ordained a Protestant minister near eighteen, and took his MA at Oxford in 1570, where Catholic leaven still worked strongly.

Warned of arrest after the Bishop of London seized a letter of his, he fled through Cornwall to Douai in 1573. After reconciling with the Church, he was ordained in 1575 and returned to the English mission in 1576, lodging with Francis Tregian in Cornwall. Arrested at Tregian's house in June 1577, he was tried that September and put to death for his priesthood, one of the early martyrs of Elizabeth's reign.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cyrene:
A historical entry describes Cyrene, a titular see of northern Africa founded early in the seventh century BC by Dorian colonists from Thera. Named for the spring Kyre, sacred to Apollo, it stood ten miles from its port Apollonia. It lay on the edge of the Green Mountains, and became chief town of Cyrenaica between Egypt and Carthage.

Prosperous under its own kings during the fifth century BC, it became a republic after 460. It then passed to the Ptolemies, and was bequeathed to Rome, becoming a colony in 74 BC.
