Many Jews lived there, and Cyrene gave the world Aristippus, Callimachus, Carneades, Eratosthenes, and Synesius. Six bishops are named by Lequien, and the Latin titular see was suppressed in 1894.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-digne:
Digne is a diocese in France covering the whole department of the Basses Alpes. It answers to the Archbishopric of Aix. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry explains how the Concordat of 1801 joined to it the old sees of Embrun, Gap, Sisteron, and Senez. Gap regained its own bishop in 1822, leaving Digne with the lands of Digne, Senez, Glandevres, Riez, and Sisteron.

Saints Domninus and Vincentius, who arrived from Africa late in the second century, first preached the faith in the old diocese. By 1905 the see counted more than one hundred thousand souls, thirty-five pastorates, and hundreds of mission churches. Hospitals, schools, and houses of religious complete a portrait of a mountain diocese at work.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-donation-of-c:
The Donation of Constantine is a forged document by which the emperor was made to grant vast privileges and lands to the pope and the Roman Church. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry explains that the oldest known copy, from the ninth century, bears the title Constitutum of the Lord Constantine the Emperor. It is addressed to Pope Sylvester the First, who ruled from 314 to 335.

In its first part, the Confession, Constantine tells how Sylvester taught him the faith, baptized him at Rome, and thereby cured his leprosy. In the second part, the Donation itself, he bestows his gifts on the Roman Church. The entry traces how scholars unmasked the forgery and why it mattered for the Roman question.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-duvergier-de-:
Duvergier de Hauranne, also called Saint-Cyran from an abbey he held, was one of the authors of Jansenism. Born at Bayonne in 1581, he died at Paris in 1643. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry follows him from humanities at home and philosophy at the Sorbonne to the Jesuit college at Louvain. There he graduated in 1604 with a thesis praised by Justus Lipsius. There he likely met Cornelius Jansen, the future theologian of the sect.

In 1605 the pair studied at Paris under the Gallican Edmond Richer, digging into Christian antiquity to restore it to honor, as they claimed, against scholasticism. Their patristic studies bore the Jansenist movement, and the entry traces Saint-Cyran's part with a long bibliography. It closes with Maynard, Faillon, and Brunetiere among his biographers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-easterwine:
Easterwine, also called Eosterwini, was abbot of Wearmouth and nephew of Saint Benedict Biscop. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry gives his birth in 650 and his death on 7 March 686. Of the noblest Northumbrian stock, he first served as a soldier under King Egfrid, son of Oswy. At twenty-four he gave up arms to become a monk at Wearmouth, then ruled by his uncle.

He was a noble youth, famed for humility, bodily vigor, and infinite gentleness, exact in rule and glad to do the lowliest work. Ordained priest in 679, he became abbot as his uncle's coadjutor in 682. When he had to reprove a fault, his tender sadness left the culprit unable to repeat it. On the day before his death, aged just thirty-six, he said farewell to all.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ecclesiastica:
Discipline, by its roots, means the shaping of one who sits at school under a master. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry notes that all Christians are disciples of Christ, seeking to form themselves in his school and by his precepts. He called himself our master, and so do we. That is evangelical discipline, but church speech has given the word other senses, which the entry lists and defines.

Discipline may be viewed in its author, its subject, and itself. In its author it is the method of framing precepts to fit the end sought, the perfect conduct of subjects, and in that sense it is called severe or mild. The entry cites Cavagnis, Hurter, and Wilmers on public church law and the treatise on the Church, guiding readers through a word of many shades.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-edmond-marten:
Edmond Martene was a Benedictine scholar of history and worship, born near Dijon in 1654 and dead at Saint-Germain-des-Pres in 1739. He entered the abbey of Saint-Remy at Reims in 1672 and was sent to train under Mabillon and d'Achery at Paris. From then on he gave his life to old books, rites, and records of monastic life.

His commentary on the Rule of Saint Benedict came out in 1690, followed by large works on ancient rites of the Church and on old monastic customs. He also gathered a vast collection of old writings on church, monastic, and civic affairs, carrying on the work of his teacher. The entry is a good guide to a monk whose patient digging shaped how later scholars read medieval worship.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-etienne-antoi:
Etienne-Antoine Boulogne, a French bishop, was born at Avignon on 26 December 1747 and died at Troyes on 13 March 1825. Poor parents raised him, and the Christian Brothers of his native city gave him his education. Talent and industry marked him, and he was ordained in 1771. His gifts as a speaker soon ranked him among Paris's most admired preachers.

Paris's archbishop barred him from preaching for a time, then withdrew the ban after Boulogne's eulogy on the late Dauphin, father of Louis XVI, won a prize. His standing as a preacher grew steadily from there. In 1786 he preached the Lenten sermons aux Quinze-Vingts, and in 1787 at the court of Versailles. One court sermon warned of the fearful storm threatening society, caused by false philosophy and irreligion. That storm broke over France sooner and more violently than foreseen, except by the keenest observers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-etienne-charl:
Etienne-Charles de Lomenie de Brienne was a French cardinal and statesman, born at Paris in 1727 and dead at Sens in 1794. He was of noble lineage, studied at the Collège d'Harcourt and then at the Sorbonne, where, despite suggestions of unorthodoxy, he received the doctorate of theology. Ordained priest in 1752, he became Vicar-General of Rouen in 1752, Bishop of Condom in 1760, and Archbishop of Toulouse in 1762.

In 1788, forced by the philosophers upon Louis XVI, he became ministre principal and Archbishop of Sens, France's second richest see. As minister he was popular with the Assembly of the Notables. But he failed to win the Parlement to his financial schemes, and fell after announcing the convocation of the States General for 1 May 1789. To offset his fall, he intrigued his way to the cardinal's hat and had his nephew Martial de Loménie made coadjutor of Sens.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-facundus-of-h:
Facundus was a sixth-century bishop of Hermiane in North Africa. He defended the Three Chapters, writings by three theologians condemned in the East. When Emperor Justinian pressed for their condemnation, Facundus refused to comply. He wrote Pro Defensione Trium Capitulorum, a twelve-book defence of the chapters.

His stand cost him exile from his see for several years. Later works attacked the emperor's later teaching on Christ's nature. He also wrote against a bishop who had yielded to imperial pressure. Facundus stands as a firm voice for conscience against state power in church affairs.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-fort-wayne:
Fort Wayne is a diocese in northern Indiana, carved out of the Diocese of Vincennes by the Holy See on 22 September 1857. It began with 20,000 Catholics, 14 priests, and 20 churches across 17,431 square miles. John Henry Luers, a German immigrant ordained at Cincinnati in 1846, became its first bishop in 1858, founded parishes and missions, built a cathedral. He provided a home for orphans before dying suddenly in 1871.

His successors kept building: Joseph Dwenger, consecrated in 1872, led the first American pilgrimage to Rome and promoted parish schools, while Joseph Rademacher remodelled the cathedral in 1896. Herman Alerding took over in 1900. The entry closes with the religious orders at work in the diocese, from the Holy Cross fathers at Notre Dame to several communities of sisters.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francois-mari:
Francois-Marie-Benjamin Richard de la Vergne, born at Nantes on 1 March 1819 and dead at Paris on 28 January 1908. He was Archbishop of Paris through the bitter church-state struggles of the Third Republic. Educated at Saint-Sulpice, he became secretary to Bishop Jacquemet at Nantes in 1849 and vicar-general from 1850 to 1869. He became Bishop of Belley in 1871, where he began the beatification cause of the Cure d'Ars, coadjutor to Cardinal Guibert of Paris in 1875. He succeeded Guibert on 8 July 1886 and was made cardinal in 1889.

 Politically attached by esteem to monarchist Catholics, he obeyed Leo XIII's 1892 call to rally Catholics to the Republic by founding the Union of Christian France. It was to unite Catholics solely in defence of religion, a union monarchists opposed and the pope finally dissolved. He defended religious congregations against the coming Law of Associations, and Leo XIII wrote to him on their behalf in December 1900.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-franz-mone:
Franz Mone, born at Mingolsheim near Bruchsal in Baden on 12 May 1796 and died at Karlsruhe on 12 March 1871, was a German historian and archaeologist of tireless energy. Schooled at Bruchsal, he entered Heidelberg in 1814 and became tutor in history in 1817. He was secretary of the university library in 1818, extraordinary professor in 1819, ordinary professor in 1822, and head of the library in 1825. From 1827 to 1831 he taught at Louvain, then edited the Karlsruhe Gazette, and in 1835 became archivist and director of Baden's General National Archives, retiring in 1868.

His early history works suffer from a tendency to trace all things possible to a Celtic origin. But his literary histories matter more: an introduction to the Nibelungenlied, a history of heathendom in northern Europe, editions of Otnit. Sources and researches on German literature and language, studies of the heroic legend, and a survey of older Dutch popular literature complete the list.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gesellenverei:
Gesellenvereine, German Catholic societies for young men's religious, moral, and professional growth, owe their shape to Adolph Kolping, the Journeymen's Father. Born poor on December 8, 1813, Kolping learned shoemaking and knew workmen's hardships on journeys, in factories, and in city lodgings. Drawn to priesthood at twenty-three, he reached ordination only in 1845 after years of study amid trouble, privation, and sickness.

As Elberfeld chaplain he found journeymen carpenters' choral society growing into a Young Workmen's Society, and as president in 1847 he gave it the Gesellenverein's marks: religious union plus mechanical skill. At Cologne from 1849 he founded a society with free instruction and a hospice for traveling journeymen, then preached the model through Germany, Austria, Switzerland, and Hungary. At his death in December 1865 some 400 branch unions stood; by 1901 they numbered 1,086, with 80,000 journeymen and 120,000 masters, and now over 1,170 unions gather under Cologne's central union.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gilbert-bourn:
Gilbert Bourne was the last Catholic Bishop of Bath and Wells, who died at Silverton in Devonshire in 1569. An Oxford man and fellow of All Souls, he held preferments under Henry VIII and Edward VI while staying Catholic at heart. Under Mary he received absolution from Cardinal Pole in 1554 and was consecrated bishop that April. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows his firm stand under Elizabeth.

As bishop he worked for the Catholic restoration, yet treated heretics with kindness, and none seem to have been executed in his diocese. Mary named him Lord President of the Council of Wales, but Elizabeth soon removed him from posts of trust. He refused to consecrate Parker and rejected the Supremacy Oath, and deprivation followed. In June 1560 he entered the Tower as a close prisoner, where he spent three years.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giorgione:
Giorgione, born Giorgio Barbarelli at Castelfranco in or before 1477, died at Venice in the autumn of 1510. Little is known of his life, and even his birth has been disputed. In Venice he studied under Giovanni Bellini beside Titian, soon outstripped his master, and broke with the timid traditional style of the day. A Catholic Encyclopedia article hails him as the joyous herald of the Renaissance.

He painted portraits in a new modern manner, full of dignity and silvery color, and he pioneered landscapes with figures and small genre pictures made for their own sake. His glowing, melting color, broad handling, and decorative aim soon marked the whole Venetian school. He worked in tempera glazed with oil, giving his pictures brilliance and permanence, and he set the fashion for frescoed house fronts in Venice.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giotto-di-bon:
Giotto di Bondone was a Florentine painter and founder of the Italian school of painting, born most probably in 1266 at Vespignano near Florence, who died at Milan in 1337. Nothing is known of him until he was thirty, and Vasari's tale of Cimabue finding him as a shepherd boy drawing sheep is, the article says, a pretty fancy. A Catholic Encyclopedia article refuses him a miraculous birth for Italian art.

The thirteenth century already teemed with renewal, from the Cosmati marble workers to the mosaic men of the Florence Baptistery. Giotto did not create that renewal, but it reached its highest expression in him, first found at Assisi in 1294 in the train of Cimabue. A friend of Dante and Petrarch, he painted Dante's portrait often. He loved life, and left a satire on holy poverty. He married and had eight children.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giovanni-anto:
Giovanni Antonio Pordenone, often called Licinio or Regillo, was an Italian painter born at Pordenone in 1483, who died at Ferrara in January 1539. Most of what is known of him comes from Carlo Ridolfi, including the tale of a grocer's commission painted between the start and end of one High Mass. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows a fresco painter in demand across the north.

His early frescoes fill churches around Pordenone, and later work took him to Mantua, Cremona, Treviso, and Venice. In 1536 he decorated three halls for the Council of Ten, though those Venetian works have perished. He knew perspective better than most contemporaries, drew well, and threw himself into church decoration with strong religious conviction. He died at Ferrara while working for Duke Ercole II, possibly poisoned, possibly of a chill or epidemic.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giovanni-bene:
Giovanni Benedetto Castiglione was a painter and etcher born at Genoa in 1616, who died at Mantua in 1670. In Italy he was called Il Grechetto for his beautiful coloring, and in France Il Benedetto. A Catholic Encyclopedia article presents an artist who probably never met Van Dyck, but studied his works and Rubens's at Genoa.

He traveled through Italy, painting in nearly every large city, and in 1654 the Duke of Mantua gave him rooms in his palace and a pension. His specialty was animal painting, though he also won praise for landscape, history, and portraits. His rank rests above all on etching. More than seventy free, spirited plates, in pure line like Rembrandt's, use light and shade that often mimic aquatint.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giovanni-da-p:
Giovanni da Piano Carpine was a Franciscan born at Pian di Carpine near Perugia in 1182, who probably died in 1252. A companion of Caesar of Spires on the second Franciscan mission to Germany in 1221, he helped found houses of the order and served as provincial in Saxony and Spain. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows his embassy to the Mongols, the first of its kind.

In 1245 Innocent IV sent him to the princes and people of Mongolia to check their invasions and seek their conversion. Setting out early in 1246 with interpreters, he crossed Russia and the Tatar frontier to Karakorum, reaching it in mid-July. The new Khan Kuyuk answered the pope with proud independence, demanding submission instead. Carpine brought home priceless knowledge of the Far East and a remarkably accurate written account.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giovanni-fran:
Giovanni Francesco Commendone was a cardinal and papal nuncio born at Venice in 1523, who died at Padua in 1584. After studies in humanities and law at Padua, he came to Rome in 1550, where Julius III made the learned young scholar one of his secretaries. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows a diplomat trusted with England, Germany, and the Netherlands.

In 1553 Julius sent him to Queen Mary Tudor to treat for the restoration of Catholicism in England. By chance he found an old acquaintance at court and won a secret interview. He carried Mary's letter and her wish to restore the faith back to Rome. In 1560 Pius IV sent him to Germany to invite Catholic and Protestant estates to the reopened Council of Trent, beginning at Vienna in January 1561.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giovanni-moro:
Giovanni Morone was a cardinal and Bishop of Modena, born at Milan in 1509, who died at Rome in 1580. His father was chancellor of Milan, and Clement VII named the twenty-year-old Giovanni to Modena in 1529. A rival claimant seized the see, and the dispute lasted until 1532, when Morone bought him off with a yearly pension. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows a negotiator of the front rank.

Under Paul III he served as envoy to Milan in 1535 and as nuncio to Ferdinand, King of the Romans, pressing for a council in Germany. He attended the diets of Hagenau, Ratisbon, and Spires. He stood among moderates who saw faults on both sides of the Lutheran struggle. When Sadoleto was denounced for a courteous appeal to Melanchthon, Morone wrote him in sympathy, against those who made religion out of hatred of Lutherans.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giovanni-perr:
Giovanni Perrone was a Jesuit theologian born at Chieri in Italy in 1794, who died at Rome in 1876. After a doctorate at Turin he entered the Society of Jesus in 1815, a year after its restoration by Pius VII. He soon taught theology at Orvieto, then dogmatic theology at the Roman College. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows a teacher whose lectures ran to dozens of editions.

Driven to England by the Roman Republic of 1848, he returned after three years of exile to his Roman chair, teaching until old age stopped him. He advised congregations, opposed the errors of Hermes, and took part in the discussions that led to the definition of the Immaculate Conception. His Praelectiones Theologicae reached a thirty-fourth edition in nine volumes, and its compendium reached forty-seven editions in two.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gunther-of-co:
Cologne's Archbishop Günther, consecrated in April 850, won an unhappy fame as the churchman who bent canon law to King Lothair II's divorce. A Frankish noble praised for ability, he first resisted giving his suffragan Bremen to St. Ansgar of Hamburg, yielding only when Nicholas I settled the matter about 860, and he served Lothair as arch-chaplain.

At Aachen synods in 860 and 862 Günther forced Queen Thietberga's confession and then let Lothair marry his concubine Waldrada. He carried the Metz synod's approval to Rome in 863. Nicholas rejected it, excommunicated and deposed him, and though Günther later regained Cologne and then lost it again, he died in 873 after a public retraction admitted him only to lay communion.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hermits-of-st:
The Hermits of St. Augustine, generally called Augustinians, are a religious order formed in the thirteenth century by joining several monastic groups under one name and the Rule of St. Augustine. They must not be confused with the Augustinian Canons. From small Italian brotherhoods they grew into a worldwide order that preached, taught, and carried missions across Europe and beyond.

Their story runs from the union of the hermit groups, through schools and preaching in the later Middle Ages, to the shock of the Reformation. Luther and other Saxon Augustinians left then, and many houses emptied. The order then turned firmly to parish work and missions, sending members to the Americas, Asia, and Australia. Readers get a full sweep of foundations, reforms, branches, and mission fields.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-history-of-me:
This sweeping article tells the history of medical science as part of the general history of civilization, starting from its Greek foundation. Modern medicine rests on Greek work, the entry argues, even though the Greeks learned much from Egypt and India and absorbed it so fully that its origins rarely show. Greek medicine began with a purely religious character, with Apollo as founder and his son Aesculapius as healing god.

From temple healing at Epidaurus and Cos, the story runs through Hippocratic medicine, Alexandrian anatomy, and Roman writers. It continues through Arab transmitters and medieval schools to Renaissance anatomists and Harvey's account of the circulation of the blood. Later chapters follow microscopists such as Leeuwenhoek, the discovery of small blood vessels and blood corpuscles, and the anatomists and physiologists who built modern medicine on experiment.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hugh-of-digne:
Hugh of Digne was a Franciscan friar and ascetical writer, born at Digne in south-east France at an uncertain date and dead at Marseilles about 1285. His close friend Salimbene, to whom most knowledge of his life is owed, calls him one of the most renowned clerics of the world. He was a great preacher favoured by clergy and people alike, fluent of speech and trumpet-voiced.

Salimbene says hearing Hugh preach felt like hearing another Paul or Elias. Joinville records Hugh's visit to King Louis IX. The king was so moved by his preaching that he tried to keep him at court, but the friar refused and resumed his preaching tours. On one such journey he wrote to John of Parma at Greccio, prophesying the deaths of pope and Bonaventure and the extinction of the Templars.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jacques-brida:
Jacques Bridaine, a preacher, was born at Chusclan in France on 21 March 1701 and died at Roquemaure on 22 December 1767. After study at Avignon's Jesuit college, he went into St Charles of the Cross's Seminary of the Royal Missions. His gift for speaking showed itself before ordination, and even the catechetical lessons he gave stirred listeners to interest and emotion.

While he was still in minor orders, he preached Lent at the church in Aigues-Mortes, where he first tried his odd methods. His great youth brought mockery, and on Ash Wednesday the church sat empty. Unshaken, he put on his surplice and rang a bell along the main streets, calling people to come and hear him. Curiosity drew a huge crowd, and his preaching kept hold of them.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jacques-paul-:
Priest and publisher Jacques Paul Migne was born at Saint-Flour on 25 October 1800. He died at Paris on 24 October 1875. After college courses he studied theology at Orléans. While a student there he briefly taught a fourth class at Châteaudun college. He was ordained priest in 1824. The next year he became pastor of Puiseaux in the Orléans diocese. A pamphlet, De la liberté, clashed with his bishop, Brunault de Beauregard.

Migne resigned his parish and went to Paris. There in the same year he founded L'Univers Religieux, later L'Univers. He meant it as a journal free of political tendency, concerned with Catholic interests alone. He edited it until 1836 and wrote very many articles for it. Meanwhile he conceived a plan to publish the Church Fathers in vast, affordable series. That plan became the Patrologia, his life's monument. The entry follows a parish priest turned publishing giant.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-de-la-fo:
Jean de La Fontaine, a French poet born at Château-Thierry in 1621 and dead in Paris in 1695, is best loved for his Fables. Eldest son of a deputy-ranger, he tried the Oratory for eighteen months, left religious life, studied law, and married in 1647 to a union that soon broke apart.

La Fontaine first published an imitation of Terence in 1654, then won a pension from Fouquet, sending a short poem each month as receipt. At the Luxembourg from 1664 he knew Molière, Racine, and Boileau, and issued his Tales, the first six books of Fables, and the novel Psyché. His animal tales still teach morals with wit and ease.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-lejeune:
Jean Lejeune, a French Oratorian preacher born at Poligny in 1592 and died at Limoges in 1672, was famed for holiness and for preaching. His energy in mission work earned him the name Missionary of the Oratory, and blindness from age thirty-five added the name Blind Father.

Son of a Dole lawyer, Lejeune was raised by his widowed mother, studied at Dole, and joined Bérulle's Oratory in 1614. After directing the Langres seminary he gave himself wholly to missions among the poor. Blindness struck while preaching Lent at Rouen in 1627, yet never stopped him. Bishops sought him for Lent and Advent, and the crown used him to win back Protestants.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-racine:
Jean Racine, a French dramatist born at La Ferté-Milon in 1639 and dead in Paris in 1699. He lost his parents young and was raised through Beauvais college and Port-Royal, where by sixteen he read Greek at sight and wrote odes in Latin and French.

Racine's first plays, Thébaïde in 1664 and Alexandre, mattered little. Andromaque in 1667 made him famous, followed by his sole comedy Les Plaideurs and the tragedies Britannicus, Bérénice, Bajazet, Mithridate, and Iphigénie. After Phèdre failed in 1677 he quit the stage for twelve years, returning only for Esther in 1689 and Athalie in 1691 at Madame de Maintenon's request.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jeanne-fontbo:
Jeanne Fontbonne, in religion Mother Saint John, second foundress of the Sisters of Saint Joseph of Lyons, was born in 1759 at Bassens and died at Lyons in 1843. She entered a new Joseph house at Monistrol in 1778, took the habit next year, and showed rare skill in schools.

Elected superior six years later, Mother Saint John aided the founder, helped open a hospital, and worked among Monistrol's girls. Refusing the Civil Constitution oath with her bishop, she held her post until a mob seized the convent, then endured prison at Saint-Didier. She was saved from the guillotine only by Robespierre's fall the day before her set execution. She rebuilt the congregation after the storm.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jerome-besoig:
Jérôme Besoigne, a French Jansenist writer born in Paris in 1686 and dead in 1763, was ordained in 1715 and took a Sorbonne doctorate three years later. He served as assistant head of Plessis College until defending Jansenism and opposing the bull Unigenitus forced him to resign.

In 1729 the Sorbonne struck Besoigne from its doctors, and Paris exiled him in 1731, though he returned the next year. His books include a six-volume History of Port-Royal Abbey and lives of four bishops in its case. Two Scripture works harmonise Wisdom books and the apostles' letters, and the latter was reprinted in Migne's complete course.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-rathbo:
Joseph Rathborne was an English priest and controversialist at Cowes on the Isle of Wight. Born at Lincoln in 1807, he studied at Ushaw and St. Edmund's, Old Hall, and was ordained in 1830. That November, Bishop Bramston sent him to Cowes, where he spent the rest of his short life. He died there in 1842.

Writing as Alethphilos, Rathborne published letters on prayers for the dead, on Good Friday and Easter, and addressed to Isle of Wight Protestants. He also wrote replies to critics and to Gladstone on Church and State. Under his own name he issued The Clergy of the French Revolution. The entry notes his name is sometimes wrongly given as Rathbone.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-schwan:
Joseph Schwane was a German theologian who wrote the first Catholic history of dogma. Born at Dorsten in 1824, he studied at Münster, was ordained in 1847, and continued at Bonn and Tübingen. He taught church history and moral theology at Münster and succeeded Berlage in Münster's dogmatic theology chair in 1881; Leo XIII made him a domestic prelate in 1890.

Schwane's chief work, Dogmengeschichte, covered the whole history of Christian doctrine in four volumes from 1862 to 1890. He also wrote on contracts under civil law, on justice and social duties, and on special moral theology. Smaller studies treat divine foreknowledge, heretical baptism, and the Eucharistic sacrifice. He died at Münster in 1892.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jules-verne:
Jules Verne was the French novelist who brought science into adventure fiction. Born at Nantes in 1828, he began with a little play and Poe-like novelettes in the Musée des Familles. A Drama in the Air, about a madman loose in a balloon, drew notice, and his publisher Hetzel urged him to stick to the new kind of novel he had found.

Verne's tales, from Around the World in Eighty Days to Twenty Thousand Leagues under the Sea and Journey to the Centre of the Earth, charmed readers in every language. France, tired of pale Dumas copies, welcomed his fresh adventures. He lived and died a Catholic, and none of his books, the entry notes, offends good taste or morals.

catholic-encyclopedia-1913-monastery-of-: Obazine, the Cistercian abbey of the Corrèze, was founded by St. Stephen in the 1100s and became a center of monastic reform. St. Catherine's Monastery at the foot of Mount Sinai has kept its lamps burning since the 500s, guarding the world's oldest library after the Vatican's. This entry covers its foundation, its treasures, and its monks. Fifteen centuries at the burning bush.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-monte-vergine: Montevergine's abbey crowns its mountain with the Black Madonna that has drawn pilgrims for nine centuries. catholic-encyclopedia-1913-montefiascone: Montefiascone, the papal summer town above Lake Bolsena, is famous for its wine and the legend of Est! Est!! Est!!!. This entry covers its diocese, its history, and its churches. The popes' lakeside retreat, where cardinals summered above the volcanic lake.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-moses-of-chor: Moses of Chorene wrote the History of Armenia that gave the Armenian people their past, from legendary kings to his own 400s. This entry covers his work, the debates about his date, and his towering place in Armenian letters. The father of Armenian history.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nazarene: Nazarene was both Jesus's title, from his hometown, and the name of early Jewish-Christian sects. This entry examines its biblical uses, its sectarian history, and its meaning. A name with two histories: the title of Jesus and the sect that bore it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-none: None is the midday hour of the Divine Office, the ninth hour when Christ died. This entry explains its psalms, its history, and its place in the monastic day. Prayer at the heat of noon: its name gave us the word for midday.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-odoric-of-por: Odoric of Pordenone was the Franciscan who walked to China and back in the 1300s, dictating the marvels he saw. This entry traces his journey, his account, and his beatification. The friar who reached Cathay: his marvels entertained medieval Europe.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ostracine: Ostracine was a city of ancient Egypt important enough to host a Christian bishop, and its see survives today only as a titular one. This brief entry notes its site and its early church history. A quiet name from the Nile delta.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-paul-gabriel-: Paul Gabriel Antoine was the Jesuit whose moral theology textbook trained generations of confessors. This entry covers his career, his Theologia Moralis, and his influence. The confessor's handbook: its well-worn pages guided confessors faithfully for a full century and more.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-peter-of-auve: Peter of Auvergne was the Paris master who completed Aquinas's commentaries on Aristotle. This entry covers his career, his works, and his school. The continuator of the Angelic Doctor: his great Aristotle commentaries on the Physics long taught medieval Paris.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-philippine-ro: St. Philippine Duchesne carried the Sacred Heart's mission to the American frontier. This entry traces her voyage, her schools, and her sanctity. The woman who prayed at the Missouri's edge: her devoted Potawatomi called her the woman who prays always.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pie-pelicane-: Pie Pelicane is the tender stanza of the Adoro Te Devote, hailing Christ the loving Pelican. This entry explains its text, its authorship, and its place in Eucharistic devotion. The hymn of the wounded breast: its pelican feeds its young with blood.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pierre-lagren: This biographical entry profiles Pierre Lagrené, a French Jesuit of the 1600s, tracing his career, his writings, and his place as the 1913 editors recorded it. A compact life from the encyclopedia's Jesuit gallery, preserved among its learned 17th-century fathers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pietro-gianno: Pietro Giannone was the historian whose Civil History of Naples defied the papacy. This entry covers his career, his history, and his exile. The Gibbon of Naples: his defiant history cost him his beloved homeland and his freedom forevermore in exile.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-constant: Constantine was the Syrian pope who journeyed to Constantinople in 711. This entry traces his pontificate, his voyage, and his firmness. The pilgrim pope of the East: his daring voyage awed the Eastern emperor himself in person at his court.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-valentin: Valentine was the pope of 827 whose forty days left barely a trace. This entry notes his brief pontificate and the scant records. The pope of a single autumn: his unanimous election pleased all of Christian Rome in 827's autumn.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-portland-main: Portland became the diocese of Maine's Catholics. This entry covers its bishops, churches, and institutions as of 1913. The faith in the Pine Tree State: its fine cathedral serves the whole Maine diocese today in living Catholic faith and prayer.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-priene: Priene, the Ionian city of the Maeander valley, once had a Christian bishop. This brief entry notes its ruins and its early church history. A silent name from Asia Minor: its Greek theater stands in marble ruins today in Turkey.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-renaud-de-bea: Renaud de Beaune was the archbishop of Bourges and Sens. This entry notes his career, his works, and his place as the 1913 editors found him. A prelate of the wars of religion: his ready pen served the League in Paris.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-richard-byrne: Richard Byrne was the American priest of the early republic. This entry notes his ministry, his works, and his place as the 1913 editors found him. A pastor of the young dioceses: his brick church rose in the American town.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-richard-langh: Richard Langhorne was the lawyer-martyr of the Popish Plot. This entry notes his trial, his constancy, and his death. The barrister of the scaffold: his learned plea failed the plot of Oates in 1679's winter of lies and fear and hate.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ripatransone: Ripatransone became the diocese of the Picene hills. This entry covers its bishops, its churches, and its history. The faith of the Marche town: its old cathedral crowns the hill of the Marche in Italy's east in stone and faith.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-robert-blackb: Robert Blackburne was the English priest of the penal mission. This entry notes his ministry, his sufferings, and his place as the 1913 editors found him. A laborer of the secret vineyard: his hidden chalice hid in the house of the recusants.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-robert-mannyn: Robert Mannyng of Brunne was the Gilbertine poet of the chronicle. This entry notes his Handlyng Synne, his verse, and his life. The minstrel of the moral tale: his rhymed verse taught the people of Lincolnshire's villages and towns in the 1300s.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rule-of-st-au: The Rule of St. Augustine is the charter of the canons. This entry explains its text, its followers, and its spirit. The brief rule of the bishop of Hippo: its brief lines guide the canons Regular in community and prayer.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-engelbe: St. Engelbert of Cologne was the murdered archbishop. This entry traces his rule, his assassination, and his cult. The martyr of the German princes: his martyr's blood stained Gevelsberg in 1225's November morn of the ambush in the wood of the road.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-jean-de: Saint-Jean-de-Maurienne became the diocese of the Savoyard Alps. This entry covers its bishops, its cathedral, and its history. The faith of the Maurienne valley: its old cathedral crowns the town of Saint-Jean in Savoy's Alps in the mountains of the east.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-john-da: St. John Damascene was the theologian of the holy images. This long entry examines his doctrine, his Fountain, and his influence. The last Father of the East: his great Fountain watered the Church in the 700s' decades of the East.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sierra-leone: Sierra Leone became the vicariate of West Africa's peninsula. This entry covers its missionaries, its churches, and its history as of 1913. The faith of Freetown: its Catholic missions dot the peninsula in the 1860s' decades in the colony of the British.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-simon-le-moyn: Simon Le Moyne was the Jesuit of the Huron missions. This entry traces his journeys, his martyrdom, and his fame. The apostle of the Onondaga: his long journeys filled New France in the 1650s' missions in the woods of the Iroquois.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sophene: Sophene, the Armenian land of the upper Tigris, once had a Christian bishop. This brief entry notes its site and its early church history. A quiet name from the East: its high hills dot Armenia in the south of the kingdom.

common-sense-thomas-paine:
Thomas Paine published his 47-page pamphlet on January 10, 1776, when many American colonists still hoped to make peace with Britain. Paine argued the opposite: the colonies should declare independence. He wrote for ordinary readers rather than lawyers or members of an assembly.

Plain, blunt language carries his case against monarchy and hereditary rule, and against the idea that a distant king in Britain should govern America. V1 evidence notes it sold by the hundreds of thousands and pushed opinion toward revolution. Few short pamphlets have changed public debate so quickly, and its title states Paine's method exactly: appeal to what readers could see for themselves.
confiscation-an-outline:
William Greenwood wrote Confiscation: An Outline to put a radical scheme of political economy before ordinary voters in plain words. Greenwood complains that economists write a dismal science only for scholars, when in a republic the voter alone can enact change. He sets his scene in the America of the 1890s: one man with fifty million dollars, another without money for shoe repairs, and parties divided among silver, protection, and free trade.

Reviewing the Populists, Republicans, and Democrats, he finds none offering escape from poverty amid wealth. His outline argues for confiscation, the taking of unearned gains for the public, as the honest name for the remedy. The pamphlet is Georgist-era agitation at pamphlet length, earnest, statistical, and aimed at the ballot box.
cymbeline:
William Shakespeare's late romance Cymbeline plays out in ancient Britain, in this old-spelling text from the same electronic Shakespeare set. King Cymbeline's daughter Imogen has secretly married the poor gentleman Posthumus, whom the king banishes. In Rome, the villain Iachimo wagers he can seduce her and steals proof from her bedroom.

Iachimo inventories the mole on her left breast, cinque-spotted like cowslip drops, to convince Posthumus of her guilt. Lost princes, a wicked queen, Roman invasion, and Imogen disguised as a boy tangle until the final scene unties every knot. Shakespeare mixes tragedy, pastoral, and fairy tale here, and the result, long undervalued, now charms audiences with its improbable grace.
do-and-dare-a-brave-boy-s-fight-for-fort:
Do and Dare, a brave boy's fight for fortune by Horatio Alger Jr, opens at the post office in Wayneboro. Alger seats Herbert Carr beside his mother in their plain cottage and lets the boy wish aloud that they could keep the office. Herbert's father held it before them, glad of the work because a war wound had cost him an arm, leaving little he could do that needed two hands.

The accounts book on the table shows a modest income for the year past, yet men still scheme for the place. Word comes that a movement is afoot to install Ebenezer Graham instead. Later chapters promise Herbert's chance, a prodigal son, the loss of his place, and Eben's scheme. Alger's pattern holds: a small public trust, a greedy rival, and a boy whose honesty must find him a larger life than Wayneboro offers.
doctor-therne:
Doctor Therne, by H Rider Haggard, is a novel written as an argument about vaccination. Haggard dedicates it to the Jenner Society, named for the pioneer of smallpox vaccination, frankly admitting he never asked their permission. His author's note attacks a government that, in a single evening, surrendered to anti-vaccination agitation and threw away the findings of royal commissions and the medical profession alike.

The story opens with a diligence journey and a Mexican hacienda, then moves through Sir John Bell, a trial, and a chapter called Crossing the Rubicon. Jane meets Dr Merchison as a red headed man arrives and the shadow of pestilence falls. A final chapter named Harvest counts the cost. Haggard uses a doctor's career, and a community's sickness, to make his case that refusing vaccination is not a private choice but a public danger.
doctor-thorne:
Anthony Trollope published this Barsetshire novel in 1858, as the title page here records, and set it in the village of Greshamsbury. The Greshams are old county family, encumbered and proud. Dr. Thorne, the village doctor, lives with his niece Mary, whose birth is the parish's open secret and whose fortune depends on the will of the ruined railway baron Sir Roger Scatcherd.

Frank Gresham, the heir, loves Mary Thorne and is told to marry money. The contents map the siege: matrimonial prospects, sentence of exile, the doctor drinking his tea, and Miss Dunstable, the rich ointment heiress Frank is pushed toward. Sir Roger's will makes Mary a prize the county had scorned. Trollope keeps the love story plain and lets pride, debt, and one honest doctor carry the book.

dora-thorne:
Charlotte M. Brame, who wrote as Bertha M. Clay for much of her career, opens Dora Thorne with a father forbidding a marriage. Lord Earle tells his son Ronald, nineteen and in love, that Dora Thorne, the lodge-keeper's daughter, can never take his mother's place. Ronald answers that love levels caste and he will marry no one else.

Brame builds her popular melodrama on that clash between rank and affection. Dora is pretty, modest, and barely educated; the Earles are proud and rich; and the consequences of folly, as the first line warns, seldom end with the one who commits it. Brame wrote for the great story-paper audience of Victorian Britain, and Dora Thorne became one of her most reprinted tales of love across the class line.
down-the-ravine:
Charles Egbert Craddock's Down the Ravine opens under a new moon in the Cumberland Mountains. A red fox barks on a ledge, imprudent, for Tennessee pays a dollar for his scalp and ears. Young Birt Dicey's rifle flashes, and the fox dies on a cliff forty feet up. Birt will not leave a dollar lying there.

The climb, and what follows, entangle Birt in a feud over counterfeiters' hidden gold and his widowed mother's farm. Nate Griggs jeers at his ambition: all the foxes in a protracted meeting could not buy a horse. Craddock, the pen name of Mary Noailles Murfree, wrote Tennessee mountain life from its own speech. The dialect is dense, the scenery grand, and the boy's dollar starts a chain of danger, suspicion, and honour satisfied. Local colour fiction rarely came more authentic.
east-lynne:
Mrs Henry Wood wrote East Lynne, a bestselling sensation novel presented here in an 1883 New York edition from John B Alden. The story opens with William, Earl of Mount Severn, gouty and short of money in his town house. His beautiful daughter, Lady Isabel Vane, is his chief treasure. Lawyer Archibald Carlyle of West Lynne comes to buy the East Lynne estate.

Carlyle marries Isabel and brings her home as mistress of East Lynne. Barbara Hare, who loves Carlyle herself, watches from the sidelines. A local murder charge, a charming villain, and Isabel's jealousy drive the plot toward ruin and remorse. Wood fills forty-seven chapters with disguise, suffering children, and deathbed scenes. Readers get the Victorian sensation novel at full stretch: secret sin, patient endurance, and moral judgment on every page.
facino-cane:
Honore de Balzac's Facino Cane, translated by Clara Bell and others, begins in the Rue de Lesdiguieres. The young narrator lives in a garret there. He studies at the Bibliotheque d'Orleans and walks the Boulevard Bourdon. At a working-class wedding he meets an old blind Venetian musician who claims a famous name: Facino Cane, prince and adventurer, who says he can see gold through walls.

The old man leads him along the Bastille ditches, unerring as a sighted man, telling of Venetian prisons, a murder, and buried treasure in the lagoon. Balzac compresses a novella of obsession into a few pages; the blind fiddler's gold-sight becomes the narrator's own creative fever. The tale opens his Scenes from Parisian Life like a whispered confidence.

from-sand-hill-to-pine:
Bret Harte filled From Sand Hill to Pine with six California tales. The title story opens on a stagecoach stopped by a fallen tree. The spot is the same one where robbers struck six months before. Driver Yuba Bill, the express messenger, and a coachload of passengers argue in the rain while axes are fetched. Snapshot Harry's niece arrives in that first tale. govdocs-archive_org-nsia-GuinnGene_Guinn:
James Ewell reported on a killing in Oak Cliff, the Dallas neighborhood where Officer Tippit died. A private security guard was charged in the shooting death of a youth he had tried to apprehend at a drugstore. The guard was moved to the county jail for his own security.

A guard charged with killing the person he stopped raises the oldest questions about private force: who may detain, and with what right to shoot. Moving the accused for security shows how hot the neighborhood felt the case. Ewell's article preserves the charge as local readers first read it.

govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_nuclear-:
A four in the morning phone call to a colonel named Odom became a byword for nuclear false alarms. William Burr edited this briefing book, number 789, published in March 2022. It carries new information on false missile alerts and threat assessment conference calls from 1977 to 1980.

The set also publishes, for the first time, the 1976 United States-Soviet agreement on NUCFLASH messaging, the emergency channel for nuclear incidents. False alerts are where nuclear safety stops being theory. Operators had minutes to decide whether warning signs meant attack or error. Documents on how those calls were handled show the human layer inside the alert machinery.
greville-fane:
Henry James began Greville Fane with a telegram: the novelist Mrs. Stormer is dying, and a newspaper wants half a column, letting her off easy, but not too easy. The narrator, a journalist who knew her, goes to the house off Primrose Hill and finds her daughter, Lady Luard, already managing the occasion. From there James reconstructs the career of Greville Fane, the pen name under which Mrs. Stormer poured out popular romances.

She wrote, the tale shows, to purchase her children's place in the society her novels vulgarly praised, and they spent both money and mother. James tells it with dry pity: the books were bad, the sacrifice real, the gratitude nil. It is his sharpest short study of the literary marketplace and family ingratitude.
harlequin-and-columbine:
Harlequin and Columbine, by Booth Tarkington, opens on Fifth Avenue in the season's most crowded week. Horse Show, football's climax, and the opera's opening fall together. Talbot Potter, the great actor manager, walks to rehearsal through the crowds. He feels the northward current's eyes on his face like surf. His Fifth Avenue knows its Talbot Potter, Tarkington says. It catalogues everyone and replaces them on the shelf.

Potter is this novella's Harlequin, a star playing at ordinary life. Columbine waits in the theatre world behind him. Tarkington knew Broadway from inside his own successes. He renders its vanity with affection and precision. The famous man's walk to work becomes a meditation on being watched. Fame, in this little comedy, is a costume that fits too well to remove. The pierrot of the title must remember he is also a man.
hebbel-herodes-und-mariamne:
Herod's jealous love for his wife Mariamne poisons his court, his reason, and finally her life. Hebbel's Herodes und Mariamne, given here in German, turns the biblical tyrant into a study of power corrupting love itself. Herod orders her death if he should fall, twice, rather than leave her to another man.

Suspicion feeds on silence, and silence feeds suspicion, until the trap closes. Mariamne's pride answers his with a fatal dignity of her own. Hebbel strips the old story to a pure clash of two unbending souls. The result is among the most intense psychological dramas in German. Few plays show so clearly how a ruler's love becomes his kingdom's curse.
honorine:
Honore de Balzac's Honorine, translated by Clara Bell, opens with a paradox about travel. The French hate it, the English love it, and both have reasons. France's charms, Balzac says, are hardest to find outside France. The narrator, consul at Genoa, tells how his neighbor the Countess Octave de Bauvan vanished from her husband and lives hidden near his own garden, behind cypresses four feet high.

Madame Gobain announces the fair neighbor one fine morning, and the count's long campaign to win back the wife who cannot forgive his youthful betrayal unfolds through intermediaries. Balzac dedicates the tale to Achille Deveria. Honorine's refusal, argued with real theological weight, makes this one of his most debated studies of marriage and conscience.
how-i-found-livingstone:
Henry M. Stanley's How I Found Livingstone, in this abridged edition, begins with a telegram in Madrid. On the sixteenth of October 1869, word came from James Gordon Bennett of the New York Herald: come to Paris on important business. Stanley, fresh from the carnage at Valencia, packed within hours. His instructions were to find and relieve Dr. Livingstone in Central Africa.

The narrative follows the expedition from Zanzibar through swamp, famine, and desertion to Lake Tanganyika. Four months' residence with Livingstone follows the famous meeting at Ujiji. Stanley prints journals, letters, and the doctor's own accounts of his wanderings. His dispatches made both men legends and opened central Africa to European readers. The book is adventure journalism of the highest polish, and its hero-worship of Livingstone never hides the reporter's own endurance and drive.
john-keble-s-parishes-a-history-of-hursl:
John Keble's Parishes is Charlotte M. Yonge's history of Hursley and Otterbourne in Hampshire, printed in 1898. Yonge calls herself an old inhabitant of the place she describes. An earlier history by the Reverend John Marsh, curate of Hursley, appeared in 1808. Ninety years of change, she explains, made a fresh book needful.

Yonge keeps what she can of Marsh's careful work while adding new findings. She gives Otterbourne the fuller treatment Marsh denied it. The careers of John Keble, the clergyman and poet, and Sir William Heathcote stand at the center. She also records three churches built since 1837 and the parish changes around them. It is local history written from inside the parish.
legends-of-charlemagne:
Thomas Bulfinch retold the Legends of Charlemagne for general readers. The book forms part of his famous Bulfinch's Mythology. It stands beside The Age of Fable and The Age of Chivalry.

Charlemagne and his paladins ride through these medieval romances. Roland, Oliver, and other knights face Saracen armies and magic. Bulfinch smooths wild old poems into clear, lively prose. A publisher's preface praises his wide learning and patient care. Generations of readers first met Europe's legends in Bulfinch's retellings. Orlando's madness and Rinaldo's feats appear in these pages. Bulfinch keeps the marvels, yet trims the medieval sprawl.
life-and-adventures-of-calamity-jane:
Marthy Cannary, known as Calamity Jane, tells her own life story here. She says she was born in Princeton, Missouri, on May 1, 1852. Her family crossed overland to Virginia City, Montana, in 1865. The five-month trip filled her days with hunting and hard travel.

Jane recalls learning to ride the wildest horses while still a girl. She rode with the men whenever excitement or adventure offered itself. By the journey's end she was famed as a fearless rider and shot. Her plain-spoken memoir feeds the legend of the wild frontier West.
little-wars-a-game-for-boys-from-twelve-:
H. G. Wells explains his game of toy soldier battles here. Contents move from the legendary past to modern little warfare. Rules cover the country, the move, and each arm's mobility. Hand-to-hand fighting and capturing get their own sections.

The Battle of Hook's Farm shows the rules in action. Extensions and amplifications invite players to grow the game. An appendix compares Little Wars with the military Kriegspiel. Wells calls it the game of kings for humbler players. Soldier sizes and battle varieties receive practical sections. A sort of challenge ends the book's main text.
living-alone:
Stella Benson published this whimsical novel with Macmillan in 1920. A first edition had appeared the year before. Benson warns that this is not a real book at all. It does not deal with real people, she insists playfully.

Real books for real people already crowd the world, she jokes. Her little alien book serves the magically inclined minority. Chapters open with magic coming to a committee meeting. The committee then comes to magic in chapter two. The Pall Mall Gazette let Benson reprint her Mad 'Bus incident. An Athenæum poem called Detachment also joins the fifth chapter.
locrine:
This lamentable tragedy tells of Locrine, eldest son of Brutus. It discourses the wars of the Britains and the Huns. The Britains' victory and Locrine's death close its action. Five acts, each with a prologue, structure the play.

Ate, goddess of revenge, heads the list of persons. Scenes move between palaces, camps, riverbanks, and battlefields. The river afterward called the Humber recurs throughout. Catalogues credit Shakespeare, though scholars doubt his hand in it. Gwendoline's camp and Locrine's camp face each other in Act Five. An epilogue closes the tragedy after the field of battle.
lore-of-proserpine:
Lore of Proserpine is a 1913 book of tales and reflections by Maurice Hewlett. Its title names Proserpine, the queen of the dead in Greek myth. Hewlett writes about the fairy kind, who go where Fate drives them. Pieces here include 'The Windows,' 'A Boy in the Wood,' and 'Harkness's Fancy.'

The book mixes short tales with musings on an unseen world near our own. Hewlett treats fairies not as cute toys but as powers bound by Fate. His prose is dreamy and old-fashioned, full of woods, windows, and chance meetings. Readers who like folklore and fantasy will find a strange, quiet charm here. It stands apart from his better-known historical novels.
lorna-doone:
Lorna Doone is R. D. Blackmore's romance of Exmoor, published in 1869. Its hero is John Ridd, a strong and plain-spoken farmer. As a boy he meets Lorna, a girl held among the outlaw Doones. The Doones raid and rob across the moor, and their valley is feared by all.

John's love for Lorna grows as the feud between farmers and Doones deepens. The tale brings raids, rescues, and a fight for Lorna's freedom and name. Blackmore fills the book with moorland weather and old West Country ways. It became one of the best-loved English romances of its century. Its mix of love, danger, and landscape still draws readers.
margot-asquith-an-autobiography-two-volu: Margot Asquith wrote her own life story in this autobiography, issued by Project Gutenberg with both volumes joined in one text. The title page gives her name and the two-in-one form, and little more can be checked here. The hosted sample holds only the old Gutenberg header pages. This note therefore stays with the title facts and claims nothing about the memoir's contents.
married-life-its-shadows-and-sunshine:
Married Life; Its Shadows and Sunshine was printed at Philadelphia in 1852. T. S. Arthur wrote the book as a guide to a good marriage. His preface calls marriage the highest and purest bond in life.

Arthur says most strife comes from hasty and ill judged matches. He urges patience, kindness, and care for each other over pride. Couples who learn those habits, he argues, can turn a strained home toward peace. The preface frames the whole book as aid for homes in strain. Arthur writes for both the ill matched and the well matched pair.
mary-erskine:
Jacob Abbott wrote Mary Erskine as one of his Franconia stories. Harper printed it in New York in 1850. His preface lays out how he hoped such tales would shape young hearts.

Abbott says example moves a child far more than rules do. A kind word to a bird can plant kind ways for life. His tales show calm home scenes, with little direct preaching, and let the acts speak. The farm scene on the front page fits that calm aim. Franconia tales like this one taught through home life, not through fear.
master-sunshine:
Mrs. C. F. Fraser wrote Master Sunshine, a tale for young readers. Seven chapters run from Who He Was to A Happy Ending. The hero's real name is Frederick Alexander Norton, called Freddy.

His mother says he chose his bright name as a baby. His smiles and laugh spread cheer long before he could talk. His sister Lucy calls him buzzer, and the cook calls him an angel. Fraser shows his kind deeds on rainy days and Sundays at home. A rainy day, a Sunday with father, and brave deeds fill the heads. Each small act shows why the whole house leans on his cheer.
maurice-tiernay-soldier-of-fortune:
Charles James Lever wrote Maurice Tiernay, Soldier of Fortune, dated 1855. Downey of London reissued his novels in 1898, with pictures by A. D. McCormick. The heads start in the days of the guillotine.

A restaurant, the Temple prison, and the night of the ninth Thermidor follow. Tiernay must choose a life, then learn the army of sixty years past. A short scene in the record shows the poor home of Pere Michel. One small room, two chairs, and a charcoal pan made his whole hearth. A scrape and its results close the heads shown in the sample. Lever mixes camp life, Paris plots, and a young soldier's luck.
memories-of-hawthorne:
Rose Hawthorne Lathrop published this family memoir in 1897. She was the daughter of novelist Nathaniel Hawthorne and his wife Sophia. Much of the book is built from Sophia's own letters, written from girlhood in 1820 until her death in 1871. Lathrop edited them into a portrait of both parents.

The opening chapters trace the Hawthorne and Peabody families and the couple's courtship. Readers meet Emerson and other Boston literary figures in passing. Lathrop writes plainly that few of her mother's pages deserved cutting. The result is an intimate record of a famous writer's home life, told by the family who lived it.
memories-of-jane-cunningham-croly-jenny-:
The Woman's Press Club of New York City published this memorial volume in 1904. It honors Jane Cunningham Croly, the journalist known by her pen name Jenny June. Caroline M. Morse edited the book. It is dedicated to the General Federation of Women's Clubs in America.

Inside are a brother's memories, speeches from a joint Sorosis and Press Club memorial meeting, and tributes from clubs across the country. Together they trace Croly's career in newspapers and her central role in the women's club movement. The volume shows how fellow writers and clubwomen judged her work while her influence was still fresh.
meyer-us4389981-hydrogen-gas-injector-sy:
United States Patent 4,389,981, granted to Stanley A Meyer on June 28, 1983, covers a hydrogen gas injector system for engines. Meyer claimed his water fuel cell split water into a burnable gas mix. The patent is one of eight in his water-fuel family held here.

The design feeds hydrogen gas into a standard engine in place of gasoline. Drawings and claims lay out the injector, its mix, and its controls in full legal detail. Patents prove a design was new on paper, not that it worked. In 1996 an Ohio court found Meyer's fuel claims fraudulent.
nasa-tm-19640007776-infrasonic-waves-fro:
Kaichi Maeda of Goddard Space Flight Center and Tomiya Watanabe wrote this paper. Watanabe was at the University of British Columbia. Their subject is infrasound, sound too low in pitch for ears to hear. Such waves had been linked with magnetic storms and auroras.

The authors propose that pulsing aurorae make these long pressure waves. Heating of the air near a set height is their favored mechanism. That height matches where auroral shimmering had been reported by others. The paper works out the energy links for the idea. It ties lights in the polar sky to slow waves that sensors can catch far away.
nasa-tm-19650019828-models-of-uranus-and:
Ray T Reynolds and Audrey L Summers, in the Space Sciences Division at Ames, built mathematical models of the planets Uranus and Neptune. No spacecraft had visited either planet. Their inner makeup had to be inferred from mass, size, and physics. The authors integrate basic balance equations on a computer to build self-consistent models.

They first estimate how likely materials behave at absolute zero. Then they plot mass against radius for model planets made of those materials. Sets of models for both planets follow from stated assumptions. The work shows what inner structures could fit the facts then known about two distant worlds.
nasa-tm-19660001387-compression-tests-on:
Lester Katz, in Marshall's Propulsion and Vehicle Engineering Laboratory, reported compression tests on cylinders stiffened as one piece in this August 6, 1965, memorandum. Such cylinders form the walls of rocket tanks and bodies. Under lengthwise load, a thin cylinder can buckle in two ways. It can fail as a whole, or wrinkle locally between stiffeners.

Katz determines the loads and stresses tied to each failure kind. Test results anchor the theory in real hardware behavior. Light, strong cylinders were vital to the Saturn program, where every pound of structure cost payload. Compression data like these told designers how thin they could safely go.
nasa-tm-19660011651-relativistic-charged:
Lawrence A Schmid at Goddard wrote this January 1966 paper, the third in a series on the flow of a charged fluid at near light speed. Part three builds a generalized Hamilton-Jacobi equation for that flow. A Clebsch transformation is applied to the problem, the catalog note says. Such equations are a compact way to state the laws that govern a moving plasma.

Relativistic plasma flow arises near extreme objects and in some fusion work. The mathematics is demanding, and each series part adds one tool. Schmid's paper is pure theory, aimed at specialists who model such flows. It shows Goddard's theoretical division working at the deep end of physics in support of space science.
nasa-tm-19670002002-mixing-and-reaction-:
Marshall C. Burrows, of NASA's Lewis Research Center in Cleveland, prepared this paper for an aerospace sciences meeting in New York in January 1967. It studies how hydrazine and nitrogen tetroxide mix and react when fired against each other. The two liquids form a propellant pair that ignites on contact, so their mixing controls rocket chamber behavior.

Burrows used a quadlet injector element, with like propellant streams placed diagonally opposite at a right angle. Photographs showed the streams breaking into spray in less than an inch. Pockets of one propellant survived four inches or less downstream. Thermocouple readings showed the hottest gases in oxidizer-rich zones, while fuel-rich gases reflected hydrazine breaking down. Spectral measurements tracked water vapor and glowing gas bands, and products appeared well mixed eleven inches or more from the injector.
nasa-tm-19670022708-solar-power-systems-:
C. M. MacKenzie, of NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland, wrote this paper in March 1967. It covers solar power systems for satellites in near-Earth orbits. Since Goddard's establishment in 1959, most of its satellites had drawn their primary electrical power from the Sun through silicon solar cells.

Solar cells alone, MacKenzie explains, often cannot deliver power at the right moments. Many orbits include eclipse periods with no sunlight at all. Other missions draw peak loads that sunlight alone cannot supply even in continuous illumination. Working systems therefore pair solar conversion with energy storage, batteries that carry the spacecraft through darkness and peaks. The paper describes several such systems in use at Goddard, including those of the IMP, Nimbus I, and ATS I satellites. Block diagrams show each system. A detailed section treats Explorer XXXIII's solar array, battery, and power control.
nasa-tm-19670027339-standard-for-color-c:
The Civil Engineering Division at NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida issued this standard on February 21, 1967. Numbered KSC-STD-S-0003 and authenticated by division chief R. P. Dodd, it sets a color code for shop machinery and equipment. The standard was mandatory for the center and its associated contractors.

The code covers shop machines, tools, and similar equipment used in interior environments only. Color coding means any painting or refinishing, from a small touch-up to a complete repainting of an item. Its purpose is emphasis: bright color highlights hazardous or critical areas on a machine so personnel notice them. Equipment that other directives require to be coated with special compounds, for outdoor exposure, heat, cold, or acids, falls outside this standard. Referenced documents include a Navy color application manual, federal primer and enamel specifications, and the federal standard color list.
nasa-tm-19680008747-cooled-baffle-develo:
E. William Conrad, John P. Wanhainen, and Jerome K. Curley, at the Lewis Research Center in Cleveland, tamed a rocket part in this report. Baffles calm the combustion inside the M-1 engine, but they sit in brutal heat and must be cooled. The team developed cooled baffles using a smaller stand-in rocket.

The subscale engine matched the full M-1 in chamber pressure and mixture ratio. Its baffle compartment size also matched, so the heat environment was realistic. The team tested a long series of baffles with several cooling schemes. One design met the requirements with good durability. Transpiration-cooled baffles misbehaved unexpectedly and were ruled unsuitable.
nasa-tm-19680016292-measurements-of-the-:
Harold E. Taylor, K. W. Behannon, and N. F. Ness of Goddard Space Flight Center report magnetic field measurements behind the Moon in this paper. Explorer 35, in lunar orbit, measured the interplanetary magnetic field near the Moon. Explorer 33 made matching measurements away from the Moon at the same time.

The team found no shock waves in front of the Moon or close behind it. The field seemed to flow past the Moon with little distortion. A regular pattern of small ripples appeared inside the lunar wake, typically under three percent of the background field. Sharp field changes seen by Explorer 33 appeared nearly undistorted in the wake records.
nasa-tm-19690008659-results-of-magnetic-:
Masahisa Sugiura of Goddard Space Flight Center reviews magnetic surveys of the magnetosphere and nearby regions in this January 1969 paper. He presented it at an October 1968 symposium in Washington on describing Earth's magnetic field. The magnetosphere is the bubble of space ruled by Earth's magnetism, and spacecraft had only just mapped much of it.

Sugiura reports that the bubble's boundary and its outer bow shock shift position often. The tail behind Earth stays well defined eighty Earth radii out, and seems to persist a thousand radii back in wake-like form. A weak-field neutral sheet splits the tail's two halves. Storm-time ring currents and a quiet-time proton belt round out the survey.
nasa-tm-19700004913-d-region-radio-measu:
J. A. Kane of the Goddard Space Flight Center wrote this NASA technical memorandum in November 1968. It reports radio measurements of the D region made right at the magnetic equator. The D region is a low layer of the upper air, and its electrons change how radio waves travel.

Kane draws on two ARCAS rocket flights launched at Thumba, India, on March 8, 1968. Electron density profiles came from watching how much the radio signals faded as they crossed Earth's magnetic field. The introduction notes that mid-latitude results were already fairly well known, while equatorial ones were not. Steady weather near the equator also made it a clean place for the study.
nasa-tm-19700010501-an-improved-method-f:
James L. Zurasky of the Marshall Space Flight Center and Robert Forsten of Sperry Rand issued this report on January 5, 1970. It presents a sharper way to measure how thick a thin film is. Thin films are very shallow layers laid on a base, used in optical filters and electronic circuits.

The older method photographs light fringes from an interferometer and measures how far they shift at an etched step. That reading covered a wide area and gave accuracy of only about fifty to one hundred angstroms. The new method scans the photo negative with a microdensitometer instead. It uses only the sharpest small area, so fringe positions can be fixed far more closely.
nasa-tm-19700017797-microscopic-coupled-:
R. J. Ascuitto of Yale University led this study, with W. F. Ford and R. C. Braley of the Lewis Research Center and J. Bar-Touv of Ohio State University. They presented it at an American Physical Society meeting in April 1970. It models what happens when protons strike neon-20 nuclei.

In such hits, a proton can bounce off and leave the nucleus in a higher energy state. That outcome is called inelastic scattering. The team used a coupled-channel method, which tracks several possible outcomes at once. Their model works at the microscopic level, building the nucleus from its parts rather than treating it as a plain sphere.
nasa-tm-19700018037-the-generation-of-x-:
Klaus Schocken of the Marshall Space Flight Center wrote this report on February 12, 1970. It asks how planetary nebulae could give off X rays. A planetary nebula is a shell of gas shed by a dying star.

Schocken sums up how these nebulae evolve and how they produce radiation, drawing on published work. Their steady glow comes from free electrons losing energy near ions, he notes. That process explains their radio output and part of their visible light. If the nebulae also emit X rays, he argues, the same process would most likely make them.
nasa-tm-19700026472-mission-training-pro:
The Mission Training Section at the Manned Spacecraft Center in Houston prepared this internal note. It sets out the training program for the third crewed Apollo mission. The section's chief, Jon J. Van Boekel, signed the program, which crews followed for months on simulators and checklists before they flew.

One strand puts crew members inside real spacecraft tests as participants, not just observers. Another strand runs the briefings, reviews, and meetings that fill the schedule between practice flights. Separate briefing series cover the command and service module systems and the lunar module systems. Launch vehicle and guidance program briefings follow, along with photography and the extravehicular mobility unit, the backpack suit system.
nasa-tm-19700030449-the-prediction-of-co:
K. H. Schatten of the Goddard Space Flight Center wrote this preprint in September 1970. It treats the prediction of magnetic fields in the Sun's corona and in the space between the planets. Those fields shape the solar wind and can disturb radio links and spacecraft far from the Sun.

Fast computers and better solar knowledge, Schatten notes, had made eclipse structure predictions possible. He discusses the magnetic field models behind such forecasts, their uses, and their limits. Solar activity's effect on coronal shape gets its own treatment. Recent work by other solar researchers, showing the surface field tracks the field between planets, points to a practical way of forecasting that wider field.
nasa-tm-19710005374-optimization-of-self:
Bernard J. Hamrock and David P. Fleming of the Lewis Research Center wrote this paper for a March 1971 gas bearing meeting in Southampton, England. It finds the best designs for self-acting herringbone journal bearings. The goal is the greatest radial load the bearing can carry.

A computer program worked out the optimal bearing for each case. The authors turn the results into design curves that cover a wide range. The curves span calm, thick gas films and highly squeezed ones. Either the smooth part or the grooved part may be the one that turns. Bearings of this kind serve in fast, clean machines where oil cannot go.
nasa-tm-19710021715-the-nasa-quiet-engin:
James J Kramer of the Lewis Research Center wrote this paper for a fall 1971 engineering meeting in Los Angeles. It introduces the NASA Quiet Engine Program. The program folded all known noise reduction methods into one propulsion system. The target was a power plant fit for subsonic civil transport aircraft. Jet noise had become a public and political problem by then.

Full scale experimental hardware was being built for the program. Tests focused mainly on noise performance, not thrust. Kramer reported the program as still in progress. Component tests finished so far pointed in an encouraging direction. The work aimed to prove a complete quiet engine, not just quiet parts. Airlines and regulators both watched for usable results.
nathaniel-hawthorne:
George E. Woodberry wrote this life of Nathaniel Hawthorne, the American novelist and story writer. Woodberry dated his preface at Columbia College on April 1, 1902. He built the book from Hawthorne's own writings, his note books, and family accounts by his son, daughter, and son in law.

Chapters move from Hawthorne's first years to the chamber under the eaves where he wrote. Later chapters cover his work as weigher and gauger, the Old Manse years, and The Scarlet Letter. Woodberry also thanks friends who let him quote their own memories. The result is a careful early life of a major American author.
nocturne:
Frank Swinnerton dated his Nocturne December 1917, and dedicated it to Martin Secker. The contents divide the tale by hours, like music played at night. Part one is Evening, with chapters named Six O'Clock, The Treat, Rows, and The Wish. The shape promises one night told in full.

Part two, Night, brings The Adventure, The Yacht, and Mortals. Penalties and What Followed lead to a chapter called Cinderella. Part three is Morning, starting with After the Theatre. Swinnerton lets a single night carry love, risk, and shame, then shows the morning after. The contents alone trace a fall and a reckoning.
old-cookery-books-and-ancient-cuisine:
William Carew Hazlitt wrote this history of old cooking in 1902. It appeared in the Book-Lover's Library series in London. Hazlitt begins by noting man's dislike of raw food. He contrasts human cooking with the habits of animals. Fruit, salads, and oysters form rare exceptions, he says.

The book surveys old cookery books and early ways of eating. Hazlitt writes with humor about game kept until very ripe. He traces taste, custom, and table manners over centuries. Food lovers gain a guide to early recipe books. The work blends food history with bookish charm.
old-times-at-otterbourne:
Charlotte Mary Yonge wrote this village history in 1891. Warren and Son printed the second edition in Winchester. Otterbourne is a Hampshire parish near the River Itchen. Yonge feared the oldest memories would soon be lost. She records life before railroad, church, and penny post.

She traces a Roman road and a Roman medallion there. The name likely means village of the otters, she says. Saxon kings, bishops, and parish bounds shape the story. The metadata note stresses her church faith and huge output. The book preserves local memory in warm, careful detail. It suits readers of English village history.
on-the-firing-line:
Anna Chapin Ray and Hamilton Brock Fuller wrote this novel. Chapter one opens aboard a ship at sea. Harvard Weldon is tall, broad, and sure of himself. He pursues talk with his table neighbor, Ethel Dent. She answers him with dry, cool indifference at first.

Weldon has spent three days trying to break her reserve. A careless waiter first gave him his opening chance. Her chaperon, Miss Arthur, lies horribly seasick nearby. Its title points from shipboard flirtation toward war. Ray writes bright dialogue with a romantic edge. He jokes that a past football hurt once broke his collar bone. Mild walks after lunch are his doctor's firm advice, he adds.
over-the-border-acadia-the-home-of-evang: Eliza B. Chase's Over the Border is a travel and history book about Acadia. Longfellow made that Nova Scotia country famous as Evangeline's home. The hosted sample shows the title page, contents, and a chronology's start only. The contents promise the Bay of Fundy and the Basin of Minas. Port Royal, Halifax, and Grand Pré follow. The chronology opens in 1604. No narrative page appears.
patriarchal-palestine:
A. H. Sayce, professor of Assyriology at Oxford, wrote Patriarchal Palestine for the Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge. The book studies the land of the Bible in the age of the patriarchs. A map at the front marks the chief places named in Genesis and Exodus.

Sayce tests the biblical picture against the records of Egypt and Assyria. The text works through Egyptian king lists, including the dynasties reported by Manetho, and the wars of Theban princes. His aim is to show what archaeology and ancient inscriptions can confirm, correct, or add to the story told in Genesis.
podcast-tuckercarlson-L28k2FTSENE:
Doctor Mary Talley Bowden is a Texas physician who clashed with her hospital and regulators during the Covid years. She joins Tucker Carlson to argue that vaccines became politicized. She also argues that the medical industry destroyed its own credibility in the process. Her account is personal as well as polemical: she describes being punished for her treatment choices and public statements.

Carlson treats her story as a case study in institutional coercion. Bowden's views on Covid treatment remain contested by the medical mainstream, and her claims are preserved here as her own.
