The episode documents a real rift: doctors who believe the profession traded trust for obedience, speaking to an audience that largely agrees. Listeners can hear the dissenting physicians' movement explain itself, in the voice of one of its most litigated members.
poems-by-emily-dickinson-series-one:
Emily Dickinson published almost nothing while she lived, and the first series of her Poems introduced her work to the public after her death. Dickinson wrote in seclusion at her family home in Amherst, Massachusetts, packing short, intense lyrics with dashes, slant rhymes, and startling images of nature, death, and faith. Only a handful of her poems appeared in print before she died, out of nearly eighteen hundred found among her papers.

Editors prepared this first volume from her manuscripts so that friends and curious readers could finally meet the work whole. The shock of the style was part of the event: hymns bent out of shape, thoughts compressed to a few lines, a voice unlike any other in American poetry. Every later Dickinson collection builds on the opening this series made.
poems-of-paul-verlaine:
Paul Verlaine's poems appear in English in this volume translated by Gertrude Hall and pictured by Henry McCarter, with a portrait of the poet at the front. Verlaine, the French symbolist whose musical, melancholy verse reshaped modern poetry, is represented by his three most famous early collections. Hall's translations keep the French titles for the sections while rendering the poems themselves into English song.

Fêtes Galantes opens the book, with Clair de Lune, Mandoline, and the Colloque Sentimental, moonlit scenes of lovers in powdered dress. La Bonne Chanson follows, love poems written for a young fiancée, all hearth light and summer days. Romances sans Paroles closes with the wordless songs, including the famous poem where it weeps in his heart like rain on the city. English readers of the period met the essential Verlaine in this handsome, illustrated form.
proportional-representation-applied-to-p:
T. R. Ashworth and H. P. C. Ashworth proposed a new electoral system in a book printed in London by Swan Sonnenschein in 1901. The elder Ashworth led the Victorian branch of an Australian free trade and liberal group.

Chapters set out the true rules of representation and attack the faults of party government. Two plans are then detailed, the Hare system and the free list system, both built on delegation in line with votes. A closing chapter applies the reform to Australian law-making bodies. Readers get a full scheme for fairer voting.
quincy-adams-sawyer-and-mason-s-corner-f:
Quincy Adams Sawyer and Mason's Corner Folks, a picture of New England home life by Charles Felton Pidgin, was published at Boston by C. M. Clark Publishing Company in 1905 in a revised edition. Pidgin dedicates the book to the memory of James Russell Lowell, whose poem The Courtin' gave him the idea for the story.

In his preface Pidgin notes that his hero's only title is plain "Mr.," though his ancestors were tradesmen, merchants, lawyers, politicians, and Presidents. He aims to make Quincy live up to an ideal of gentlemanly qualities, and argues that the New England standard for a novel's hero should stand as high as Old England's.
quotes-and-images-from-the-works-of-mich:
Quotes and Images from Michel de Montaigne takes its quotations from the five volumes of the Essays, with five etchings promised at the head of the selection. David Widger sets the great French essayist's sentences in alphabetical order, a Montaigne for browsing.

A child should not be brought up in his mother's lap, and a generous heart ought not to belie its own thoughts. A man may govern himself well who cannot govern others, may play the fool in everything but poetry, and never speaks of himself without loss. A little cheese makes a feast when the mind is set, and a well-bred man is a compound man.
real-soldiers-of-fortune:
Richard Harding Davis profiles men who fought for hire or for causes not their own, and his book opens with Major-General Henry Ronald Douglas MacIver. MacIver may be met, Davis says, on Fifth Avenue, gray-haired and stiffly erect, with a sabre cut across his forehead. His titles ran from ensign in India to general of brigade in Servia.

Born at sea off Virginia on Christmas Day, 1841, MacIver was schooled at Edinburgh and sent to India at sixteen. He fought in the Indian Mutiny, took a sword cut through helmet and towel into his skull, and was left for dead. He next wore Garibaldi's red shirt in Italy, and few later wars lacked him.
reymont-the-comedienne:
Wladyslaw Reymont tells of a young woman who flees dull town life in The Comedienne, here in English. She joins a traveling theater troupe, hungry for art and fame. Backstage life soon shows her both its glitter and its grime.

Reymont, later a Nobel laureate, knew poverty and striving at first hand. His heroine pays for ambition with pride, love, and hard lessons. The troupe's actors, jealous, kind, and vain, ring true in every scene. The novel gives a vivid, unsparing portrait of artistic dreams in partitioned Poland, and of the price a woman paid to chase them.
rhymes-of-a-rolling-stone:
Robert W. Service gathered these verses in a book first issued in 1912, here in a printing of 1917. A comic verse at the front begs pardon for his literary sins, saying the other kind do not matter. A prelude and a title poem, A Rolling Stone, open the contents.

The Soldier of Fortune, The Gramaphone at Fond-Du-Lac, and Athabaska Dick carry the northern settings of his fame. Sunshine, Cheer, Ambition, and Dreams Are Best strike his hopeful note. Darker pieces stand beside them: The Blind and the Dead, Death in the Arctic, and The Lunger. Barb-Wire Bill and The Rover keep the wandering figure of the title in view throughout.
rodney-stone:
A. Conan Doyle's Rodney Stone appears here in an edition from Eveleigh Nash and Grayson of London, dated 1921. Doyle's preface, signed at Haslemere on September 1, 1896, lists the books he drew on for life in England at the start of the century. Gronow's Reminiscences, Jesse's Life of Brummell, and Fitzgerald's Life and Times of George the Fourth stand among them.

Boxiana and Pugilistica fed the prize-ring scenes, and Doyle thanks Robert Barr and J. C. Parkinson for facts on the ring. Harper's Brighton Road, Rice's History of the Turf, and naval lives of Collingwood and Nelson complete his shelf. Contents open at Friar's Oak, with Buck Tregellis, the Peace of Amiens, and the Brighton Road ahead.
ronicky-doone:
Max Brand published this western novel in 1921, opening at a gallop in its first chapter, A Horse in Need. A rider comes into town inside a solid cloud of dust, his horse at the last limit of strength. Dull eyes, hanging head, and sweat dripping into the white street dust mark the animal's state.

The rider is nearly as spent, a wide-shouldered, gaunt man with dust masking his face and pink skin round his eyes. He climbs the hotel steps and asks the loungers for a horse to reach Stillwater within three hours' riding. The oldest man answers first, this being a matter of life and death: any horse can do it, by the short way across the mountain.
salomy-jane: Bret Harte wrote Salomy Jane, with pictures by Harrison Fisher and Arthur I. Keller, issued at Boston and New York in 1910 by Houghton Mifflin. Copyrights of 1898, 1900, and 1910 stand on the title page. The contents list four chapters: A Kiss and an Escape, The Lady's Reflections, The Kiss Repeated, and Another Escape. The first chapter heading is repeated at the close of the pages shown here, with no narrative passage following it in this portion.
sane-sex-life-and-sane-sex-living-some-t:
H. W. Long, M.D., wrote Sane Sex Life and Sane Sex Living, an authorized edition issued in New York in 1919 by the Eugenics Publishing Company. The subtitle promises things that all sane people ought to know about sex nature and sex functioning, its place in the economy of life, its proper training, and its righteous exercise. Long gives the volume to fellow members of the medical profession and to all who may read it under their direction. A firm note asks that the book be read from beginning to end without skipping, at least on a first reading, if its purpose is to be realized.

The contents outline that purpose in plain heads. An explanatory introduction charges that wrong teachings about sex leave children brought up in ignorance on sex matters.
sanine: Michael Artzibashef wrote Sanine, translated by Percy Pinkerton with a preface by Gilbert Cannan. The contents page shown here gives press notices of the novel in place of a chapter list. The New Statesman finds a treble interest: sex problems discussed with unusual candour, a vivid picture of Russian life, and the welter of thoughts common to the whole contemporary Western world.
sarrasine:
Honore de Balzac wrote Sarrasine, presented here in English by Clara Bell and others and dedicated to Charles Bernard du Grail. The story begins near midnight at a grand Paris house party. From a curtained window seat the narrator watches two scenes at once and sets them against each other.

Outside, snow rests on the garden trees under a cloudy, moonlit sky, and the pale shapes suggest ghosts and death. Inside, well-dressed guests fill a bright salon where jewels, music, talk, and card play hold attention. The narrator lingers on the contrast between the cold, quiet garden and the warm, crowded rooms before the tale moves on.
seeing-europe-with-famous-authors-volume:
Francis W. Halsey edited this third volume of his ten-volume travel set, opening France and the Netherlands in Part One. The tourist bound for France lands at Cherbourg, Havre, or Boulogne, each port rich in recalled events. Cherbourg recalls the sea fight where the Kearsarge sank the Alabama.

An opening survey runs from Roman rule in Gaul through the growth of great ports like Marseilles. Famed writers then lead readers through towns, churches, and coast scenes. The volume pairs trip guidance with deep history, so a traveler lands knowing the ground's long past as well as its present face.

Francis W. Halsey edited this fourth volume of his travel set in 1914, carrying France and the Netherlands into Part Two. The volume centers on cathedrals and chateaux, the great church and castle sites of France. Named guides include Thomas Frognall Dibdin, H. A. Taine, and Henry Wadsworth Longfellow.

Contents list Bayeux and its famed tapestry, the chateau of Henry IV at Pau, and Loire valley seats such as Amboise, Blois, and Chambord. Each stop pairs a building's stones with the tales and rulers tied to it. Art and history lovers get a rich route through old France.
since-ce-zanne:
Clive Bell gathered these art essays around the change Cezanne wrought in modern painting. Contents move from the artistic problem and the Douanier Rousseau to Renoir, then to tradition and movements. Matisse and Picasso share a chapter, while Bonnard and Duncan Grant receive their own.

Portraits of Cezanne, Seurat, Matisse, and Picasso stand among the pictures. Later essays treat Negro sculpture, standards, and art's place in criticism, closing with jazz and M. Derain's authority. Bell writes as a champion of the new French art, arguing that form, not story, gives a picture its life.
soldiers-of-fortune:
Richard Harding Davis opens his novel Soldiers of Fortune in a New York drawing room. Mrs. Porter begs Alice Langham to come early and do her a favor at dinner. A man she barely knows needs a place at the table, and the debutantes, she says, grow cross when set next to men who cannot help them. Alice, known as good-natured, is her hope.

The guest is a cowboy friend of George's, met while shooting in New Mexico or Old Mexico. He fed George, gave him game to shoot, and now calls in New York with a letter asking to be placed. Mrs. Porter will set him next to Alice, with Reginald King on her other side. Alice's look of fun cools at King's name, and she grants the plan with stiff grace.
sterne:
H. D. Traill published his life of Sterne in 1882, working with sources he admits are thin. For the years before fame, nearly all that survives is a short memoir Sterne wrote for his daughter. He wrote it a few months before his death. It covers childhood, school days, Cambridge, and his Yorkshire vicarage.

From 1759 onward, Sterne's letters run to 1768, the year he died, and form the main record of his later life. Traill weighs the earlier attempts too. He treats Scott's brief memoir and Thackeray's lecture essay. He also credits Percy Fitzgerald's two large volumes with holding nearly all the facts now likely to be recovered. Those facts concern the author of Tristram Shandy and the Sentimental Journey.
stifter-bunte-steine:
Each story in Stifter's Bunte Steine takes its name and mood from a stone: granite, limestone, tourmaline, and others. Colored Stones, given here in German, gathers tales of family, fate, and the Austrian landscape. Children in danger and parents in prayer recur across the collection's quiet dramas.

Precise, luminous, and morally serious, the stories rank among the finest short works in German. A plague year, a mountain rescue, a foundling's fate: small events carry enormous weight in Stifter's hands. Nature is never mere scenery; it tests and shelters his people in turn. The collection makes the essential Stifter for the short-story reader. Few books prove so well that gentleness and power can share a style.
stories-from-everybody-s-magazine: Only the front pages of an old electronic text are present here. They announce stories drawn from the 1910 issues of Everybody's Magazine, dated October 1996, and carry the standard welcome and donation appeals of that early free-text project. No title page, contents list, or story text from the magazine itself appears in these opening pages.
stories-from-the-pentamerone:
Giambattista Basile's tales, known as Il Pentamerone, were first published at Naples in the Neapolitan dialect. A note at the front says Basile, Count of Torrone, is believed to have gathered the tales chiefly in Crete and Venice, and to have died about the year 1637.

The contents list thirty-two pieces, from How the Tales Came to Be Told through The Myrtle, Peruonto, The Flea, and Cenerentola, an early form of the Cinderella story. Serpents, enchanted does, dragons, the tale of Sun, Moon, and Talia, and The Three Citrons follow. These rough, witty folk tales stand among the first great printed collections in Europe.
story-of-chester-lawrence-being-the-comp:
Nephi Anderson's Story of Chester Lawrence came from The Deseret News at Salt Lake City, Utah, in 1913. It completes the account of a man who played an important part in his earlier novel. That novel was Piney Ridge Cottage. Anderson's other books include Added Upon and The Castle Builder.

The tale opens in rain at a pier, where a crowd under dripping umbrellas waves farewell to friends aboard a departing ship, and a late passenger scrambles up with heavy hand baggage. Anderson wrote fiction rooted in his Mormon faith and Utah life, and this story follows Chester Lawrence beyond the earlier book, giving his part of the tale in full at last.
sue-a-little-heroine: Only the opening pages are present here. They give a title page for Sue, A Little Heroine, by L. T. Meade, printed by the New York Book Company in 1910, followed by a publisher's biography of the author. That sketch names her as Mrs. Elizabeth Thomasina Smith, born at Bandon, County Cork, in 1854, a first book written at seventeen, and more than fifty novels after, many drawn from her studies of East London life. No page of Sue's own story appears here.
tattine:
Ruth Ogden, who also wrote as Mrs. Charles W. Ide, made Tattine a tale for young readers, built around a small girl and her dogs. Chapter one is called Trouble No. 1, and trouble is the heart of the book.

Tattine, age seven, sits in an apple tree one June morning, sketching a chime tower on a neighbor's land. Below her rest her setters Betsy and Doctor, while Doctor's granddam Tadjie lies buried near by. That day Tattine learns that some wrongs lie past even her mother's power to set right. Readers get a soft, grave child's tale about loss, love of pets, and the first hard truths of life.
tempest-and-sunshine:
Mary J. Holmes wrote Tempest and Sunshine, a novel in twenty-six chapters printed by J. H. Sears and Company of New York. Chapter one is headed Mr. Wilmot Arrives at Mr. Middleton's, and the scene is set in Kentucky.

On a bright October day at four, the Lexington and Frankfort stage rattles into the small town of V, drawn by four tired horses. It halts at The Eagle, the chief hotel of the place, as a guest steps down. Readers enter a tale of two unlike sisters, hinted by the title's storm and sun, in a once-loved American novel of love, pride, and family strife in the South.
that-fortune:
Charles Dudley Warner wrote That Fortune, a novel that starts with a boy of twelve and a tall tree on a mountain edge. Chapter one lingers on that perch before the tale moves out into the world.

The lad swings in the top of a lithe hickory, the first picket of a forest, above rocky pasture and chestnut woods. Below run orchards, cornfields, and an amber river whose murmur climbs to him like an old tale he cannot yet grasp. The wind's push and the tree's spring stir him, and ambition to make his own way stirs too. Readers follow Philip Burnett from this hilltop into wealth, law, and love, in a tale of what fortune does to a man.
the-32nd-mersenne-prime-predicted-by-mer:
The 32nd Mersenne Prime is a short math note built around one vast prime number, found by David Slowinski. It was posted in honor of Andrew Wiles' proof of Fermat's Last Theorem, news of that same week in February 1993.

A tag line gives the cost of the find: 26.562767 minutes of work using Maple 4.0 on a Cray 2 machine. The prime itself then fills the page, row on row of digits in fixed blocks. Readers get a plain record of a record-class find, showing how big-machine searches in the early 1990s pushed the hunt for Mersenne primes to new lengths.
the-acadian-exiles-a-chronicle-of-the-la:
Arthur G. Doughty wrote The Acadian Exiles, a chronicle of the land of Evangeline, printed at Toronto in 1916 as volume nine of Chronicles of Canada. That set, in thirty-two volumes, was shaped by George M. Wrong and H. H. Langton.

Chapter one, The Founders of Acadia, starts with the name itself, which may stem from a Micmac word for a camp or a rich place. The French used Acadia for the maritime east of New France, apart from Canada on the St. Lawrence. Where one ended and the other began was never set clear, a blur that later fed war with the English. Readers follow the French settlers of Acadia toward their famed exile.
the-atlantic-monthly-volume-01-no-03-jan:
January 1858, the third number of The Atlantic Monthly's first volume, leads with notes on domestic architecture. If building many houses could teach a people to build well, the writer begins, Americans ought to excel: never was there such a house-building people.

Elsewhere, he notes, laws, customs, want of capital, or want of land hold building in check, and most men either inherit a house or never build at all. Even the pattern comes down by custom, and the soil itself decides the main points: no brick without clay, no wood without forests. In America, by contrast, every man builds for himself, freely and by his own whims.
the-atlantic-monthly-volume-02-no-10-aug:
August 1858 leads with Daphnaïdes, a survey of the English laurel from Chaucer to Tennyson. Verses from Chaucer's Flowre and the Leaf head the piece, praising those who bore the crown of laurel leaves for noble deeds in their time.

The writer scolds the zeal of antiquarians who chase fanciful subjects over real ones. Young men of that bent, he says, flit bee-like from flower to flower: now an unreadable tombstone, now a rusty helmet, now crumbling old writings. Little can be hoped, he warns, from hunters so fitful, unless they settle on worthier game like the poets his survey honors.
the-atlantic-monthly-volume-02-no-12-oct:
October 1858 opens with The New World and the New Man. Half a dozen small streams leap down the west slope of the Rocky Mountains and join. Four thousand miles away the great Missouri pours into the Mexican Gulf. It is the fruit of that meeting.

Did the streams plan the river? Not at all, the essay says. Each knew only its own need to find a lower level, and a broad law did the rest. So runs human history: a lasting surprise, worked out by agents who never expected the result. Even a hound that outran a train from Lowell to Boston did so intent only on its dinner, yet served its owner's wager.
the-atlantic-monthly-volume-03-no-15-jan: Volume three of The Atlantic Monthly opens with its January 1859 number, present only as a contents list. Titles include Agrarianism, Bulls and Bears, a bundle of old letters, coffee and tea, and a piece on the differential and integral calculus. The Minister's Wooing and the Professor at the Breakfast-Table both appear. Other heads name Charles Lamb and Sydney Smith, Holbein and the Dance of Death, a plea for the Fijians, Shakespeare's art, and the question whether women ought to learn the alphabet.
the-atlantic-monthly-volume-04-no-22-aug:
August 1859 leads with the dramatic element in the Bible. The writer is careful with words: in the Bible, not of it, since the trait he means is a matter of form, not of the book's sacred core. He also disowns any tie to the playhouse and its stage tricks.

No charge of irreverence should stick, he argues. He claims only the freedom of the painter, the sculptor, and the poet. Each of them treats holy subjects by the laws of his own art. Their aim is to enrich the sacred page and honor their craft. As those arts find the picturesque, the statuesque, and the poetical in scripture, so may a critic mark what is dramatic there.
the-atlantic-monthly-volume-04-no-24-oct:
Daily Beauty, a story, opens the October 1859 Atlantic late in a city afternoon, about four o'clock. Stanford Grey and his guest Daniel Tomes rest from an earnest half-hour's argument. What they argued about, the narrator says, does not concern us.

Each man leans back sure he has held his ground, granting only the other's skill and honest purpose. They savor the slow sinking of excitement that follows the friendliest clash of minds. The narrator likens it to the calm after the gloved bouts of two famed professors of self-defence, who beat each other with padded buckskin at short intervals for some widow's benefit.
the-atlantic-monthly-volume-05-no-27-jan:
January 1860 opens a series on American artists in Italy with Hiram Powers, the sculptor. Old art, the essay holds, does more than give a standard to measure new work by. It tests whether an artist's impulse is true, a higher worth still.

Even to genius a true art-life is hard to reach. The artist faces a double mystery: the hidden self from which his fancies float like seeds from unknown shores, and the outer world that yields him means to give them shape. Clear foresight is denied him, and his errand is like that of a commander who bears sealed orders, drifting for years before he knows what he is for.
the-atlantic-monthly-volume-06-no-34-aug:
The Carnival of the Romantic opens the August 1860 Atlantic with a question: where did the nine old Muses go when their seats on Helicon, Parnassus, and Olympus were overrun? Not far, the essay answers.

They hovered like witches around the seething pot of early Christian Europe, where a new order of life was forming amid toil and trouble. They kept in mind the bright line of their worshippers from Homer to Boethius, and waited for the time when mankind would gird itself anew with beauty. They were sorrowful but not in despair, the essay says, for they knew the children of men are strong in power to recover.
the-atlantic-monthly-volume-06-no-36-oct:
Some of the Haunts of Burns, by a tourist who claims no imagination or enthusiasm, leads the October 1860 Atlantic. The party left Carlisle a little past eleven and within half an hour reached Gretna Green. From there they rushed into Scotland through flat, dreary bog where moss-troopers once hid after raids into England.

Hills rose at last, some nearly mountain high. In about two hours they reached Dumfries and got down at the station. For all Scotland's chill fame, the day was fiercely hot. They pushed through burning sunshine into town, asking the way to the house of Burns, down a street called Shakspeare Street toward one named Burns Street.
the-atlantic-monthly-volume-07-no-39-jan:
Washington City leads the January 1861 Atlantic, and paradox leads the piece. Washington, it says, is the paradise of paradoxes: a city of magnificent distances and still more magnificent gaps between seeming and being. Anything may be claimed of it, and everything denied.

Call it a city, and its empty seasons deny the name. Call it a spread-out village, and another fact denies that instead: its wards are full of decayed or callow politicians. It harbors fashion, vice, and bright minds, with drinking in abundance and gambling in any quantity, yet no waters, baths, or springs. Wall-less and moat-less, it still stands as the Sevastopol of the republic, besieged without end by contractors and claim-agents.
the-atlantic-monthly-volume-08-no-46-aug:
Trees in Assemblages leads the August 1861 Atlantic. Trees, the essay argues, cannot be used up as a subject by treating them one by one or kind by kind. Some have little charm alone and gain everything from grouping.

A lone fir or spruce by a roadside is a stiff and unpleasant object, the writer says, but a deep forest of firs is surpassed in grandeur by no other species. Elms and oaks, wide-spreading trees, stay grand standing alone in any place. The Romans, he notes, kept four words for these groupings: silva for a wood seen as timber, and other terms for wilder gatherings of trees.
the-atlantic-monthly-volume-08-no-48-oct:
Near Oxford, a travel piece, leads the October 1861 Atlantic. On a fine September morning the party sets out for Blenheim. The writer and a sculptor ride on the box of a four-horse carriage. Two more ride in the dicky. The rest are less happily placed inside.

They have no coachman. Two postilions ride in their place, in short scarlet jackets and leather breeches with top-boots. Each sits astride a horse. They bob up and down in the saddle for the riders to watch. The day is sunny and warm, a spell of perfect English weather with a mere spice of sharpness to make it sweeter. The flat country between Oxford and Blenheim, the writer admits, holds little of note.
the-atlantic-monthly-volume-09-no-51-jan: Volume nine of The Atlantic Monthly, dated 1862 in Roman numerals, is present only as a contents index keyed to issue numbers. Agnes of Sorrento runs through issues 51 to 54, and Fremont's Hundred Days in Missouri through 51 to 53. Other entries name Jefferson and Slavery, Love and Skates, a letter to a young contributor, James Fenimore Cooper, Arthur Hugh Clough, and the experiences of one A. C. in issue 52. Light literature, the sorrows of childhood, and the fruits of free labor in the smaller British West Indian islands also appear.
the-atlantic-monthly-volume-10-no-58-aug:
The New Gymnastics leads the August 1862 Atlantic. Bodily training, it says, rides the top of the wave, but so far the movement is mostly talk. Millions praise the gymnasium; hundreds seek its blessings.

Signs of bodily decay crowd in on every side. Parents watch their children with painful care, and not even fond partiality can hide decaying teeth, twisted forms, pale faces, and an unseemly gait. Husbands would give fortunes for roses in a loved one's cheeks, the essay says, while thousands fear marriage as a road to lasting invalid life. The evil is immense, and the piece presses its question: what can be done?
the-atlantic-monthly-volume-10-no-60-oct:
Autumnal Tints leads the October 1862 Atlantic. Europeans coming to America, it says, are startled by the brilliance of our autumn leaves. English poetry holds no account of such a sight, since English trees take but few bright colors.

Thomson's Autumn, quoted at length, speaks only of many-colored woods deepening to a crowded shade of dun and sooty dark under a beaming sun. The change of our woods, the essay charges, has hardly tinged American poetry either: October has scarcely entered it. Many city people have never even seen the show, the ripe fruit of the year, and one such citizen, ridden out a fortnight too late, would not believe what he had missed.
the-atlantic-monthly-volume-10-no-61-nov:
Wild Apples, subtitled the history of the apple-tree, leads the November 1862 Atlantic. No plant's history, it says, is tied more closely to man's. The apple's order, the Rosaceae, with the true grasses and the mints, reached the earth only a short time before man appeared on it.

Apples fed an unknown early people whose traces have lately been found at the bottom of Swiss lakes, older than Rome's founding, with no metal tools. A whole black, shrivelled crab-apple was recovered from their stores. Tacitus says the ancient Germans met their hunger with wild apples, and Niebuhr notes that Latin and Greek share their words for house, field, plough, wine, oil, milk, sheep, and apples.
the-atlantic-monthly-volume-11-no-63-jan:
Happiest Days leads the January 1863 Atlantic by calling out a common sigh. Long ago, it begins, every child has been scrubbed, combed, and changed into a clean apron to be shown to Mrs. Smith, Dr. Jones, or Aunt Judkins, a friend of mother's early days.

After facing a battery of questions too high or too low, and slipping gladly away, the child hears the soft sigh behind him: dear child, he is seeing his happiest days. In the concrete it is Mrs. Smith speaking, the essay says; in general it is Commonplacedom giving its verdict on childhood. No greater absurdity exists, the writer insists: he thought so as a child, and now he knows it.
the-atlantic-monthly-volume-12-no-70-aug:
An American in the House of Lords leads the August 1863 Atlantic. Having described the House of Commons and sketched its leading members in a former number, the writer now leads his readers into the Lords. He skips what was already said of the New Palace of Westminster as a whole.

What remains is the hall where the Lords sit, and it deserves, he says, a fuller notice than his limits allow. As the finest specimen of Gothic civil architecture in the world, perfect in its kind, the chamber calls for close description. The essay promises an American's fresh eye on Britain's upper house at work.
the-atlantic-monthly-volume-12-no-72-oct:
A second paper on Charles Lamb's uncollected writings leads the October 1863 Atlantic. Readers of Lamb's Life and Letters recall, it begins, that before Mr. H. was written, and before Kemble rejected John Woodvil, Godwin's tragedy Antonio was staged at Drury Lane, with Elia in the audience.

What many readers do not know concerns Lamb's essay on the artificial comedy of the last century. As first printed in the London Magazine, it carried a full account of one performance. It told how John Kemble played Antonio in that unlucky play, cold and stately. For some reason, the essay notes, Lamb never reprinted that part of the article. The paper restores and weighs the lost passage.
the-atlantic-monthly-volume-13-no-75-jan: Volume thirteen of The Atlantic Monthly, printed at Boston by Ticknor and Fields in 1864, is present only as a volume title page and the start of a contents list. The first entries name Ambassadors in Bonds by Caroline Chesebro, Annesley Hall and Newstead Abbey by Mrs. R. C. Waterston, The Beginning of the End by C. C. Hazewell, Bryant by G. S. Hillard, and a piece on California as a vineland. No article text appears in these pages.
the-atlantic-monthly-volume-14-no-82-aug:
Charles Reade leads the August 1864 Atlantic. Someone lately classed Reade with the clever writers of the day, the essay notes, sandwiching him between Anthony Trollope and Wilkie Collins. The reason given was only that he never serves gossiping drivel or tangles of plot.

Charles Reade is not a clever writer merely, the essay insists, but a great one, and only a careful survey of his works can tell how great. No one can take the place of the novelist lately lost, who touched so truly the chords of every passion. Yet now that he is gone, someone must step from the ranks, and the piece weighs Reade for that vacant place.
the-atlantic-monthly-volume-14-no-84-oct:
A Night in the Water leads the October 1864 Atlantic, a soldier's memory of picket duty in the delicious early summer of the South. Among the endless flowery forests of that blossoming isle, the writer recalls, it was a pleasant life.

In retrospect he sees himself adrift on a horse's back amid a sea of roses. The outposts spread within a five-mile radius. The whole duty was one long, delightful gallop by day and night. The moon seemed to shine steadily every night for two months. Yet he also recalls stretches of darkness so dense that riding past a walk was unsafe. Branches threatened above and roots below. One of his officers was once shot at by a Rebel scout.
the-biography-of-robert-murray-m-cheyne:
Andrew A. Bonar wrote the standard life of Robert Murray M'Cheyne, minister of St Peter's Church in Dundee, Scotland. A publisher's preface says M'Cheyne died in 1843 at the age of thirty. Few men, it claims, packed such power and blessing into so short a span.

Bonar's biography is reprinted here from a larger Memoirs and Remains, without the letters and sermons, which were issued separately. Wilbur M. Smith is quoted urging every minister, of whatever denomination, to own it. The preface sends the unabridged life out again as a challenge and inspiration, stressing a young minister wholly surrendered to God's will.
the-boy-inventors-radio-telephone: Richard Bonner wrote The Boy Inventors' Radio-Telephone, put out in New York by Hurst and Company with art by Charles L. Wrenn. The front plate shows Jack in a thrill as he sends the first spoken word ever passed between an airship and land. The chapters start with The Power of the Air and a brush with an odd soul. The Professor's Dilemma and a search come next. Chester Chadwick is named as maker, and the set gets its great test.
the-boy-scouts-on-a-submarine:
Captain John Blaine wrote The Boy Scouts on a Submarine. The first chapter is called The Unexpected Visitor. It opens on a sleepy summer day, broken by a great barking of dogs. Elinor Pomeroy lays down her knitting and walks round the house. Her brother Lester races up the long drive, dogs leaping round him, and cries for three cheers.

Lester says his invention is a success, tried and sure. At the plant he told the board what he had found: a gas of great power, hit on while testing other stuff. One grenade of it, he says, can put thousands of men into a deep sleep for hours, with no harm once it wears off. Troops could then take their ground and cart the sleepers to the rear. He means it as a kind swap for the deadly gases used by the Germans.
the-brother-of-daphne:
Dornford Yates wrote The Brother of Daphne. Its chapters bear brisk heads: Punch and Judy, Clothes and the Man, and When It Was Dark. Adam and New Year's Eve, The Judgement of Paris, and Which to Adore come next. A point of honour, The Love Scene, The Order of the Bath, and A Private View fill the late list. All Found closes it.

The tale opens in a garden patter between brother and sister. Daphne, leaning back in her long chair, says she said he'd do something. Her brother stops swinging his legs and answers coldly that she lied, darling, in her white throat. He asks if the petrol has come. The row turns on an appointment he has in Town on the fete day. Daphne smiles faintly and asks which day. The tone is light, dry, and full of family ease.
the-cave-boy-of-the-age-of-stone: Margaret A. McIntyre wrote this book for young readers, copyrighted in 1907 by D. Appleton and Company of New York. Only the title page and contents are present here. The chapter titles follow a boy named Thorn and Strongarm's family. They cover the making of stone tools, the taming of the dog, and the coming of fire. A feast of mammoth meat also appears. Later chapters turn to how such weapons were first found. A closing section gives hints to teachers. No chapter text follows.
the-courage-of-marge-o-doone:
James Oliver Curwood's The Courage of Marge O'Doone was printed in New York by Doubleday, Page and Company in 1925, under a 1918 copyright, with a frontispiece by Lester Ralph. An earlier copyright of 1916 shows the tale first ran as The Girl Beyond the Trail.

Chapter I sets a winter scene at midnight in deep December. From the edge of a bleak spruce forest, with wind moaning through twisted trees, the Transcontinental train looks like a thing of dull fire, black and still against the half-Arctic night. A band of light cuts it from first coach to last, with a gap like a break in its length.
the-court-of-the-empress-josephine: Imbert de Saint-Amand wrote The Court of the Empress Josephine, translated by Thomas Sergeant Perry and issued in an illustrated edition dated 1900. Its contents run from the beginning of the empire and the journey to the banks of the Rhine through the pope's arrival at Fontainebleau. The preparations for the coronation and the coronation itself follow. Later chapters treat palace etiquette, the empress's household, Napoleon's gallantries, the journey in Italy, the coronation at Milan, and the campaign of Austerlitz. Only the title page and contents are present here.
the-discovery-of-a-world-in-the-moone: The Discovery of a World in the Moone comes through a transcriber's note and the start of its title page. The note says spelling and punctuation follow the original. Greek words are transliterated between plus marks, Hebrew between hash marks, and Latin passages set as block quotes. A picture shows the sun with orbits, labeled for Mercury, Venus, Ceres and Proserpina, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn, with the earth and its moon below. No author is named in what is present, and the title page breaks off at its opening words.
the-experiences-of-a-barrister-and-confe:
Samuel Warren's The Experiences of a Barrister, and Confessions of an Attorney, dated 1880 in this printing, lists a barrister's casebook in its contents. Heads name The March Assize, The Northern Circuit, The Contested Marriage, The Mother and Son, and a writ of habeas corpus. Later come Esther Mason, The Marriage Settlement, The Second Marriage, and a case of circumstantial evidence.

Bigamy or no bigamy, Jane Eccles, The Chest of Drawers, and The Gentleman Beggar close the list. Warren, who wrote Ten Thousand a Year, mines real legal tangles for moral tales. Law's traps catch the proud and the poor alike.
the-exploits-of-elaine: Arthur B. Reeve's The Exploits of Elaine, a Craig Kennedy book, is present here as title matter and a contents list. Fourteen chapters are named. First heads give The Clutching Hand, The Twilight Sleep, and The Vanishing Jewels. Later ones name a death ray, blood crystals, and The Reckoning. No story text appears in these pages, beyond the first lines of chapter one at the very end.
the-firing-line:
Robert W. Chambers wrote The Firing Line as a novel whose chapter heads borrow the speech of war: a skirmish, a landing, an advance, a flank movement, an armistice. It was printed at New York in 1908.

Chambers gives the book to Margery Chambers. The war terms dress a tale of love and society as a campaign, with ground won and lost by looks, calls, and plots. Readers of his Fighting Chance knew his world of rich country houses and smart folk. Here the siege is social, but the pride, risk, and wounds are played as real as any fight.
the-firm-of-girdlestone:
A. Conan Doyle wrote The Firm of Girdlestone as an early novel, given to his old friend Professor William K. Burton of Tokyo, who first urged him to finish the tale. A diamond firm in London stands at its heart.

The contents run from a kept meeting and a sly kind of charity to a sea captain, a college election, and a corner in diamonds. Senior and junior Girdlestone pull the strings of trade and greed. Written before Sherlock Holmes made Doyle's name, the book shows his young craft: a firm built on sharp deals, a son torn by them, and crime bred in the counting house.
the-forest-of-swords-a-story-of-paris-an: Only the list of Joseph A. Altsheler's books is present here, set out as the front matter of The Forest of Swords. The page sorts his tales into series: the French and Indian War, the Young Trailers, the Texan, the Civil War, the Great West, and the World War sets. The Forest of Swords stands last in the World War series, after The Guns of Europe and The Hosts of the Air. No title page or chapter of the tale itself follows in the pages given here.
the-fortunate-foundlings-being-the-genui:
The Fortunate Foundlings tells the tale of Colonel M----rs and his sister, Madame Du P----y, children of a great house, and it was printed at London in 1744. The preface swears the tale is true.

The writer grants that false secret histories have made readers doubt all such books. This one, he vows, rests on real letters, private notes, and the words of folk deep in the events. The foundlings' strange turns of luck carry them through the polite courts of Europe. Wonder, travel, and the lives of persons of rank fill a tale meant to please and to teach the young of both sexes.
the-four-epochs-of-woman-s-life-a-study-:
Anna M. Galbraith, a doctor, wrote The Four Epochs of Woman's Life as a study in hygiene, with a note of praise from John H. Musser. Galbraith taught at the Woman's Medical College of Pennsylvania.

Musser calls the mothers of a land its bulwarks and urges all women to learn the truths in the book. A verse from Longfellow heads the work: each stone of a life rests on the one below. Galbraith guides women through the stages of life, from girlhood to old age, with plain rules on health, work, and care of the body, written when female doctors were still rare.
the-girl-and-her-fortune:
L. T. Meade wrote The Girl and Her Fortune. Its heading is dated 1906. Chapter One is called Leaving School. Sisters Brenda and Florence Heathcote have just ended their school days. Brenda is nineteen and the clever one. She loves books by Tyndale, Huxley, and Darwin. Florence is eighteen and the pretty one. She has a fine singing voice.

Both girls are orphans with no kin at all. A lawyer, Mr. Timmins, holds their funds. He has run their lives from a distance since their parents died. In the school breaks they stay with Mrs. Fortescue at Langdale, near Tunbridge Wells. She is kind but keen-eyed, and she is paid for their care. The girls feel sure a London house and a bright life wait for them. They have met none of the hard ways of the world yet.
the-go-ahead-boys-and-simon-s-mine: Ross Kay wrote The Go Ahead Boys and Simon's Mine. Pictures are by R. Emmett Owen. Barse and Hopkins printed it in New York. Only front matter is present here. It gives the title page and a publisher's list of the series. The title page quotes Davy Crockett's motto. Be sure you are right, it says, then go ahead. The series list names six books. They run from Smugglers' Island and The Treasure Cave to this volume. Each book cost 75 cents. No chapter text is present.
the-go-getter-a-story-that-tells-you-how:
Peter B. Kyne wrote The Go-Getter. Its subtitle is A Story That Tells You How to Be One. Kyne dedicates the book to his dead chief, Brigadier-General Leroy S. Lyon. Lyon preached loyalty to country and to the task at hand. Chapter I opens in the lumber world of the Pacific Coast.

Mr. Alden P. Ricks heads vast lumber and shipping firms. Men call him Cappy Ricks. He tells his managers that he has more troubles than a hen with ducklings. His son-in-law, Captain Matt Peasley, mocks the claim. Cappy snaps back that the trouble is business. In his old age he lacks men who will get things done. The tale that follows shows what a go-getter is.
the-history-of-the-telephone:
Herbert N. Casson wrote The History of the Telephone. A preface marvels at the speed of growth. Thirty-five short years had passed, Casson says. The newborn art of telephony was already fullgrown. Three million telephones stood in foreign countries. Seven million stood in the land of its birth.

Ridicule has given way to habit, Casson notes. People take the telephone for granted, as if it were part of nature. Speech with absent persons, once impossible, is now common. He promises a story that is not technical. It is not statistical, and it is not exhaustive. He names telephone leaders a second volume could hold.
the-human-machine: Arnold Bennett published this book on self-management in November 1908. It kept selling for years. The front pages list edition after edition. A sixth edition arrived by August 1913. Only the title pages and contents are present here. The chapters themselves do not appear. The contents show his program in outline. Taking oneself for granted comes first. Amateurs in the art of living follows. The brain appears as a gentleman-at-large. Later chapters treat habit-forming by concentration. Daily friction gets a chapter. Another promises rule over one's own mind.
the-inner-shrine: Harper and Brothers published this novel of today in 1909. Their offices were in New York and London. Copyright entries date to 1908 and 1909. A note warns that the author's name appears nowhere in the text. That author was Basil King. Only the title page and illustrations list are present here. The story itself does not appear. The captions sketch a society plot. A heroine named Diane props a cablegram in plain sight. A banker scans a poor little list. A Mrs. Bayford purrs to her guests.
the-jesuit-missions-a-chronicle-of-the-c: Thomas Guthrie Marquis wrote The Jesuit Missions, a chronicle of the cross in the wilderness, as number four in the Chronicles of Canada series. The pages present here, however, hold only the old Project Gutenberg etext header, so none of Marquis's narrative appears. The header identifies the file as etext number 4388, first posted on January 20, 2002, produced by Gardner Buchanan, in its tenth edition. The title and series place promise an account of the Jesuit missions in early Canada, but no chapter of it can be read in what is present.
the-life-and-genius-of-nathaniel-hawthor:
Frank Preston Stearns wrote his study of Nathaniel Hawthorne to supply a gap he saw in earlier lives. His preface notes that Hawthorne notebooks and two friends recollections long supplied the public facts. George P. Lathrop systematized them in 1872, and Julian Hawthorne fuller biography followed in 1884.

Julian, Stearns says, modestly avoided judging his father genius or examining the literary work with care. Stearns aims to do both tasks here. Readers get a life of the Salem romancer plus a critical argument about tales such as The Scarlet Letter and the notebooks behind them.
the-life-of-cicero-volume-one: Anthony Trollope wrote his life of Cicero in two volumes, and Harper issued volume one in New York in 1881. Only the title page and the start of the contents are present here, listing an introduction, Cicero education, the condition of Rome, and his early pleading for Sextus Roscius Amerinus. A chapter on Cicero as quaestor follows in the list. The biography itself cannot be read in this record beyond those headings.
the-life-of-john-milton-volume-3-1643-16: David Masson wrote his life of John Milton alongside the political, church, and literary history of the time, and volume three covers 1643 to 1649. Only the title page and detailed contents are present here, listing the Westminster Assembly, the Solemn League and Covenant, Milton unhappy marriage, and his first divorce treatise. A second book promises Marston Moor, the New Model Army, Areopagitica, and more divorce pamphlets. The biography itself does not appear here.
the-lost-lady-of-lone: Mrs. E. D. E. N. Southworth's The Lost Lady of Lone is dated 1876. What is present stops at a publishers' notice and part of the contents; the novel itself does not appear. The notice stresses that the plot is founded on thrilling and tragic events in the domestic history of a distinguished family in the Highlands of Scotland. Contents shown include The Bride of Lone, An Ideal Love, The Ruined Heir, Salome's Choice, and A Horrible Mystery on the Wedding-day, followed by discovery chapters.
the-machine:
Upton Sinclair's The Machine is a play in three acts about money and city politics. Its cast, listed in order of appearance, includes Julia Patterson, a magazine writer, and Jack Bullen, a parlor Socialist. Allan Montague, a lawyer, Jim Hegan, the traction king, Annie Roberts, a girl of the slums, and Robert Grimes, the boss, follow. The acts move from Julia's apartments in a model tenement on the lower East Side to Hegan's country place on Long Island. Then they reach his private office in Wall Street the next morning.

Act one sets Julia's living room in detail: plain arts and crafts furniture, portraits of Morris and Ruskin on the walls, book-shelves everywhere. Julia pushes back a lamp and eats a light supper while struggling with a magazine that will not stay open. Sinclair builds his drama from a reformer's small rooms facing a traction magnate's wealth.
the-maid-of-maiden-lane:
Amelia E. Barr's The Maid of Maiden Lane, dated 1900, is a sequel to The Bow of Orange Ribbon and calls itself a love story. Chapter one, The Home of Cornelia Moran, opens on New York in the bright spring days of 1791. Never, Barr writes, was the city more glad and gay: proud, opulent, and cleared of every trace of British rule and occupancy. Its homes stood restored and refurnished, and its sacred places reconsecrated.

She likens the city to a young giant on tiptoe, eager for adventure, sending ships to the ends of the world on messages of commerce and friendship. Its streets were shaded by trees, and some of the greatest men of the century walked in their green shadows. The contents promise Arenta's marriage, two proposals, misdirected letters, and a heart that waits.
the-moonstone:
Wilkie Collins's romance The Moonstone, dated 1868, is present here only through a contents list, so the famous diamond's story does not appear. The list shows a prologue, then The Story, divided into periods. Under First Period, fifteen chapters are numbered without titles before the list stops.

A sibling record of the same novel carries a much longer contents, running through twenty-three chapters of the First Period and into a Second Period of separate narratives. This record's list ends at Chapter XV of the First Period. Beyond the frame of prologue, periods, and numbered chapters, nothing of Collins's plot or narrators is shown in these pages.
the-mule-bone:
The Mule-Bone, by Langston Hughes and Zora Neale Hurston, is a comedy of Negro life in three acts. Only a contents list and a cast of characters are present here, so no dialogue appears. A transcriber's note says obvious misprints in stage directions were fixed while dialogue was left unchanged. The contents name only Act One, Act Two, and Act Three.

Character sketches do the describing instead. Jim Weston is a guitarist and Methodist, quick-tongued and self-important; Dave Carter, a Baptist dancer, is soft and happy-go-lucky. Daisy Taylor, a Methodist domestic servant, is plump, fickle, and proud of her clothes. Joe Clark, mayor, storekeeper, and postmaster, is drawn as arrogant, ignorant, and powerful, with two rival Methodist elders beside him.
the-natural-history-of-selborne:
Gilbert White's The Natural History of Selborne opens in this printing with a poem, Invitation to Selborne. The verses summon a stranger to the village's bold beauties, its varied valley and mountain ground, all wildly majestic. Nature's rude magnificence, the poem argues, shames the tasteless expense of flats loaded with ornaments.

The invitation turns practical and fanciful by turns. Plan the light, airy pavilion, swell the scant rill into a lake, extend the vista, and raise an ivy-crowned castle mound in antique taste. Evenings might pass in tea on the beech-grown hill, in a nest-like bower, or at a straw-clad hermit's cell in a leafy dell. Spire, hall, pasture, fallow, and golden grain fill the prospect the poem lays out.
the-navy-as-a-fighting-machine:
Rear Admiral Bradley A. Fiske's The Navy as a Fighting Machine is present here only in title page and a partial contents list, so the argument itself does not appear. Fiske had been Aid for Operations of the Fleet and president of the United States Naval Institute, and he held gold medals from that institute and from the Franklin Institute. A map is promised with the volume.

Contents divide the book into parts. Part I, General Considerations, runs from War and the Nations through Naval Power, Preparedness, and Defense to Naval Policy. Part II, Naval Strategy, covers designing the machine, preparing the active fleet, reserves and shore stations, and naval bases, breaking off at Operating the Machine.
the-nursery-no-106-october-1875-vol-xvii: The Nursery was a Boston monthly magazine for the youngest readers, and number 106 came out in October 1875, in volume XVIII, from John L. Shorey at $1.60 a year. Only the front matter and contents are present here, so the stories and poems themselves do not appear. Listed pieces include The Delights of the Seaside by Emily Carter, A True Antelope Story, The Pet of the Ship, and a song, Going Through the Corn.
the-nursery-no-165-september-1880-vol-28: The Nursery, a Boston monthly for the youngest readers, reached number 165 in September 1880, in volume XXVIII, from the Nursery Publishing Company at $1.50 a year. The opening leaves are all that is present: front matter plus a contents list, with none of the stories or poems themselves. The contents open with Rosa Bonheur by Alfred Selwyn and Pip and Pop by Uncle Charles, and include A Day on Grandpa's Farm, Brownie's Adventure, and a Song of the Birds.
the-nursery-no-169-january-1881-vol-xxix: Number 169 of The Nursery, a Boston monthly for the youngest readers, is dated January 1881, in volume XXIX. A note warns that pages 23 and 24 were missing from the scanned booklet. Only the front matter and contents are present here, so the stories and poems themselves do not appear. The New Year number lists That Merry Christmas by Uncle Charles, A New Year's Dialogue by Marian Douglas, and The Christmas-Tree by George S. Burleigh.
the-parson-s-daughter-of-oxney-colne:
A tale from the 1864 Chapman and Hall collection Tales of All Countries opens in Devonshire, on the skirts of Dartmoor. No author is named in the pages present. The narrator calls this the prettiest scenery in England, where the Dart, Avon, and Teign form, and praises Chagford, Manaton, and Holne Chase to doubting travelers.

In the parish of Oxney Colne stand only two decent houses. The larger is the parsonage, home of the Rev. Saul Woolsworthy and his daughter Patience, called Miss Patty. The smaller belongs to Miss Le Smyrger, an iron-willed spinster of fifty with a hundred and thirty acres, a pedigree, and an opinion on every subject. The stage is set for a country tale.
the-perils-of-pauline:
Charles Goddard wrote The Perils of Pauline. Chapter One, The Breath of Dead Centuries, opens in a stately mansion on the lower Hudson. Old Stanford Marvin, president of the Marvin Motors Company, dozes over his papers while his secretary Owen watches him. Owen, a rascal who never lies when the truth will do, wonders whether his employer will last a year or a month, since the will should hold a handsome bequest for him.

A crate from Cairo has arrived by express. Marvin orders the bust of Pallas Athene removed and the mummy he bought in Egypt stood in its place. The fainting, aging manufacturer and his scheming secretary set up the serial's mix of wealth, danger, and strange imports.
the-pilgrims-of-the-rhine:
Edward Bulwer Lytton's The Pilgrims of the Rhine, with The Ideal World placed before it, is dedicated to his brother Henry Lytton Bulwer. The dedication is dated London, April 23, 1840. It explains that the tales woven into the voyage of Gertrude and Trevylyan were largely written during a Rhine trip the brothers made together. Lytton notes the work was a favourite of his brother's and much liked abroad.

An advertisement to the first edition asks that the work be judged by the rules of poetry rather than prose. Lytton admits to giving the imagination loose rein while painting Rhine scenery and its legends. The wild German spirit, he says, shaped the telling. He also says he chose the simplest materials for the main interest on purpose. The frame of a river journey carrying inset tales follows from that design.
the-powers-and-maxine: The Powers and Maxine, a novel by C. N. and A. M. Williamson, carries a 1907 copyright and illustrations by Frank T. Merrill. The pages shown hold the title matter and the contents, so the story itself is not on view. Chapter titles follow two women through the plot: Lisa listens, Lisa makes mischief, and Lisa's knight appears. Maxine acts on the stage and off, gives back diamonds, and drives with the enemy. Ivor travels to Paris and goes into the dark, while Diana takes a midnight drive and hears news.
the-princess-aline:
Richard Harding Davis's The Princess Aline opens by bringing its heroine into a young man's life at exactly the right moment. H. R. H. the Princess Aline of Hohenwald entered Morton Carlton's life at the moment his affairs and heart were readiest for her. Three years sooner or later, she would likely have passed with only a look of admiring curiosity. Coming when she did, she led him into several wise and many foolish things.

Carlton, called Morney, had become his own master at twenty, with fine connections but no family besides a bachelor uncle. Against that uncle's wishes he left Harvard to study art in Paris. There he worked harder than men less careful of dress and manners. By twenty-six he was a portrait-painter of international reputation. The French government bought one of his paintings for the Luxembourg, and millionaires and ambassadors sat before his easel.
the-record-of-a-regiment-of-the-line: Colonel M. Jacson writes the history of the First Battalion Devonshire Regiment during the Boer War of 1899 to 1902, published at London by Hutchinson in 1908. Contents move from events leading to the siege of Ladysmith through the siege itself, an advance north under Sir Redvers Buller, Lydenburg, and trekking in the north-east Transvaal. Here only the title pages and contents list are present, so the campaign narrative itself does not appear.
the-red-one:
Jack London's collection appeared at London in 1919. Mills and Boon published it. Four stories fill the volume. The title piece leads, and tales of a hussy follow it. An Argus-like figure and a princess complete the list. The title story opens with a sick man named Bassett. He times an enormous sound with his watch. It strikes him like an archangel's trumpet.

Bassett tries for the thousandth time to analyze the tone. The peal fills a mountain gorge to overflowing. It floods earth, sky, and air. Tribal strongholds ring with it on every side. Mystery and obsession drive the scene. London's South Seas atmosphere arrives as pure sound. No explanation is offered at the start.
the-reflections-of-ambrosine:
Elinor Glyn begins with a signed note denying that she wrote two anonymous books whose titles suggested her authorship, insisting that everything she writes will carry her name. Her heroine Ambrosine then wonders whether blue blood brings real disadvantages.

Ambrosine and her grandmother pretend to enjoy unheated December bedrooms after her father's failed South American speculation ends their Paris comforts. They keep only an old nurse named Hephzibah and one servant in a small furnished cottage in England. Good breeding under reduced means, observed with wit, is the novel's opening ground.
the-revolution-in-tanner-s-lane: Mark Rutherford's novel appears in a 1913 Hodder and Stoughton sevenpenny edition. Contents move from the world outside and Pike Street through a theatre, a friend of the people, tea, Jephthah, unconventional justice, politics and Pauline, a religious picnic, and an exposition of Romans. Here only the title pages and opening of the chapter list are present, so the lane's revolution itself does not appear.
the-rich-mrs-burgoyne:
Kathleen Norris dedicates her novel to Kathleen Mary Thompson. A verse praises Thompson as a lover of books. A Wordsworth sonnet follows the dedication. It mourns plain living and high thinking lost. Rapine, avarice, and expense take their place in the poem. Chapter one drops into a busy kitchen instead. Ramekins need polishing there, and borrowed dishes need chasing.

Children, neighbors, and helpers crowd the opening talk. Helpers wait down in the cellar. The talk jumps from errand to errand without pause. Wealth will face a plain test in this house. Household disorder will test it daily. Norris grounds her rich heroine in domestic bustle first. Display comes later, if it comes at all.
the-rise-of-roscoe-paine:
Joseph C. Lincoln lets his narrator Roscoe Paine spar with housekeeper Dorinda in chapter one over a simple walk to the village. Her answering grunt, he explains, can mean almost anything on Cape Cod, and he catalogs its temperatures from Labrador cold to near-tropical warmth.

Dorinda uses the same sound to obey his mother, to dismiss a tardy fish-cleaner's excuses, and to freeze Roscoe's evasion about his errand. The joke establishes a household ruled by tone rather than words. Lincoln's Cape Cod comedy begins with small talk carrying all the weather of a place.
the-romance-and-tragedy-of-a-widely-know:
William Ingraham Russell tells his own life story, dedicating it to a wife who remains his sweetheart after more than forty years of marriage. His address to readers calls the tale unfinished and true, with tears on some manuscript pages, smiles on others, and scorch marks of indignation elsewhere.

Russell writes to honor his wife's devotion, correct public misunderstandings, expose fair-weather friendship that vanishes in adversity, and, frankly, sell the book. He warns that real names appear and disguised ones are thinly veiled, yet claims no malice. Memoir as self-vindication is announced before any events are told.
the-romance-of-elaine-sequel-to-exploits: Arthur B. Reeve continues his Craig Kennedy series here. A sequel to the Elaine exploits carries the story. Contents open with a serpent sign at the head. A cryptic ring and a watching eye follow. Wu Fang takes his vengeance in the early chapters. Shadows of war and a lost torpedo come next. A grey friar and a vanishing man follow them. A submarine harbor holds the middle of the list. Conspirators and a wireless detective close the opening chapters. Only the series heading and title page are present here.
the-rover-boys-on-the-ocean-or-a-chase-f:
A Chase for a Fortune subtitles The Rover Boys on the Ocean, companion volume to The Rover Boys at School. Arthur M. Winfield signed its introduction as Edward Stratemeyer on September 20, 1899. The earlier book showed life at a military boarding school, with its brightness and shadows, trials and triumphs, plots and contests.

The new tale adds an ocean trip. It grows from a small, unpretentious beginning into something entirely unlooked for. The outing tests the nerves of the bravest American youths. Dick, Tom and Sam and their friends must stand the test and triumph over their enemies. A following volume set in the African jungle is already announced.
the-rover-boys-out-west-or-the-search-fo:
Out West, the fourth Rover Boys volume, is subtitled The Search for a Lost Mine. Arthur M. Winfield dated his introduction June 20, 1900. He calls the tale complete in itself. He recaps the brothers' adventures at Putnam Hall, in a daring ocean rescue, and in the heart of Africa.

The new story returns Dick, Tom and Sam first to Putnam Hall. Then it takes them to the great mining district of Colorado. No trace remains of a valuable mine. The boys set out to hunt for the property, little dreaming of the perils awaiting them. Winfield promises they overcome obstacle after obstacle. They also get the best of various enemies.
the-sonnets-of-michael-angelo-buonarroti:
John Addington Symonds translated the sonnets of Michael Angelo Buonarroti and Tommaso Campanella into rhymed English, presenting them in 1878 as the first such rendering. In his prefatory note he says he kept the older English form of the artist's name on purpose. Familiar forms, he argues, carry associations that strict accuracy should not outweigh.

Symonds thanks Pasquale Villari for help with difficult passages in Campanella, and V. de Tivoli for pointing out a Michelangelo sonnet found written behind a drawing held at Oxford's Taylor Gallery. Portions of the introduction and translations had already appeared in the Contemporary Review, marking the volume as serious Renaissance scholarship for general readers.
the-story-of-a-mine:
Bret Harte dedicated this little volume, dated from New York in December 1877, to Udo Brachvogel, whose clever translations had introduced his writings to German readers. Part one opens on a steep trail over the Monterey Coast Range, where Concho rides tired, dusty, and disgusted.

Concho's one relief is a leathern bottle on his saddle, lately filled near Tres Pinos by an Irishman selling American whisky under a pleasing Castilian title. He drinks deep and makes a wry face. He surveys the barren valley behind him. A mocking white line marks the horizon. Is it the Sierras, or the cursed whisky? Then he resumes the climb toward the mine of the title.
the-touchstone:
Edith Wharton's Touchstone opens with a newspaper notice: Professor Joslin, writing the life of the famous novelist Mrs. Aubyn, begs her friends for letters from before her coming to England. Glennard drops the Spectator and stares into his club fire. The small inner room overlooks rain-streaked Fifth Avenue, and his boredom carries resentment. He fears he may soon have to surrender even this despised club, a symbol of his perpetual paring-off of expenses.

Glennard is reducing existence to keeping himself alive, yet none of his privations brings him nearer marrying the woman he loves. Across the room he watches rich, dull young Hollingsworth with contempt. Wharton sets her trap quietly: a poor man, a dead novelist's letters, and a biographer publicly asking for exactly what Glennard secretly holds.
the-trail-of-the-lonesome-pine:
John Fox Jr. opens The Trail of the Lonesome Pine with a girl sitting at the base of the big tree, sunbonnet pushed back, bare feet gathered under her crimson gown. She has climbed steeply through dewy morning from the cove to see the wonders the circuit rider described: a great glare of yellow light and a shrieking monster running without horses. All she finds is smoke trailing in the valley below, and disappointment darkens her deep eyes.

She risks a scolding, or worse, from her step-mother for the climb, yet awe at the widening world holds her dreaming. Beyond the mists, the blue mountain waves must run to the end of the world, where her dead sister had gone. Fox sets his famous Kentucky romance where the old mountain life first sights the coming railroad age.
the-true-citizen-how-to-become-one:
W. F. Markwick and W. A. Smith wrote The True Citizen, How to Become One as a supplementary reader for seventh and eighth grades, and its preface states the gap it fills. Many textbooks treat citizenship politically, but the moral and ethical aspects have been seriously overlooked. The authors searched in vain for a book joining the development of natural faculties and moral instincts into well-rounded manhood. Character, they hold, matters far more for public life than mere political instruction.

Their plan is simple: thirty-nine chapters, one for each school week. Every chapter opens with five short 'memory gems' to be learned across the week. Anecdote and incident do the teaching, with special illustrations set in bold type. The preface argues that ethics and civics must go hand in hand, a Progressive-era creed for the classroom.
the-wheel-o-fortune: Louis Tracy, author of The Wings of the Morning, published The Wheel o' Fortune with a list of his earlier successes printed alongside. Hugo's Device and The Pillar of Light number among them. The pages present here give that list and the title pages, so the novel itself does not appear. Tracy's earlier titles run to adventure and sea tales: The Lost Naval Papers, The River War, Sylvia's Chauffeur, and The White Squall. Readers learn the author's catalogue from this record, not his new story.
the-young-explorer-or-claiming-his-fortu: Horatio Alger, Jr.'s The Young Explorer, or Claiming His Fortune, is shown here through a partial contents list. Ben's inheritance opens the story in chapter one. Deacon Pitkin makes him an offer in chapter two. Ben searches for a place, then dines with a strange acquaintance. Miss Sinclair works a stratagem in chapter eleven. San Francisco and the Canon Hotel follow. The chapters themselves do not appear in the pages present.
thus-spake-zarathustra-a-book-for-all-an: Friedrich Nietzsche's Thus Spake Zarathustra, subtitled a book for all and none, appears in Thomas Common's translation. A contents list opens with an introduction by Mrs. Forster-Nietzsche. Part one begins with Zarathustra's prologue and discourses. Discourse titles include the three metamorphoses, academic chairs of virtue, backworldsmen, despisers of the body, joys and passions, and the pale criminal. Reading and writing, war and warriors, a new idol, and chastity follow. A contents listing alone is included in this record, so Nietzsche's discourses themselves are not shown.
tracks-of-a-rolling-stone: The Honourable Henry J. Coke published his reminiscences in a second edition with Smith, Elder at London in 1905, dedicated to his daughter Sybil. Coke also wrote A Ride over the Rocky Mountains and Creeds of the Day. His preface to the second edition says the first was written from beginning to end in five months, without diary or notes beyond passages cited from a former work. The preface opening is what is given in this record, so Coke's reminiscences themselves do not appear.
u-s-copyright-renewals-1950-january-june:
January to June 1950 brings the first half-year catalog in the run, headed Renewal Registrations for literature, art, and film. Works are listed alphabetically under title, musical compositions excepted. Cross-references gather every essential name tied to a work, plus variant forms of those names.

A typical entry gives the original copyright date and number, then the renewal number, renewal date, and claimant. The list opens with Martens's life of A. E. Uhe, copyrighted December 30, 1922 and renewed March 17, 1950 by a successor publisher. Abbott's Digest of the New York reports follows with four renewal numbers of its own. Most works here date from 1922 and 1923.
u-s-copyright-renewals-1951-january-june:
With 1951 the heading shortens to Renewals, and the arrangement changes. Entries now stand under main headings, whether author, editor, compiler, or title. Only Class A works, the book class, are covered in this catalog. Joint authors and editors appear as references leading to the main heading.

Each entry carries both the original and the renewal registration facts. Austin Abbott's digest of the New York reports leads off, its 1922 volumes copyrighted in May 1923. The Lawyers Co-operative Publishing Company renewed the set on April 25, 1951. A historian of legal publishing can trace how long-lived reference works stayed protected through claimant renewals like this one.
u-s-copyright-renewals-1952-january-june:
A criminal-trial manual opens the January-to-June 1952 catalog. Austin Abbott's brief for the trial of criminal cases, in a third enlarged edition by James J. Barbour, was copyrighted on March 28, 1925. Its renewal number, R96000, was registered on June 9, 1952.

The list follows the Class A plan, with main headings for authors, editors, compilers, and titles. Cross-references route joint creators to the heading where the full entry stands. Entries always give both registrations, so a reader can match a 1920s book to its 1950s renewal in one glance. Law books bulk large in this half year, as the Abbott entries suggest.
u-s-copyright-renewals-1953-january-june:
A pen name opens 1953's first half: A. E., the pseudonym of George William Russell, sends readers to the Russell heading. Abailard follows again, this time with the Abelard and Heloise letters in a full translation from the Latin. The catalog's heading language widens slightly, naming compilers among the main-heading choices.

Entries still pair original and renewal facts for every Class A work. Cross-references from joint authors and editors keep the alphabet honest, gathering scattered names at one heading. For a researcher, the value lies in the pairing: a book of 1925 can be matched to the person or firm that claimed its second term in 1953.
u-s-copyright-renewals-1954-january-june:
Austin Abbott returns at the head of the January-to-June 1954 list, this time for his digest of the New York reports for 1925. That volume was copyrighted on August 14, 1926. The Lawyers Co-operative Publishing Company again stands behind the renewal.

The catalog covers books, pamphlets, serials, and periodical contributions, filed under author, issuing body, or title. Claimant names earn cross-references of their own, a help when a publisher rather than an author holds the renewal. Legal publishing dominates these opening pages, since digests and reports were renewed as a matter of routine by the firms that issued them. Rights researchers use such entries to date a work's protected life.
u-s-copyright-renewals-1955-january-june:
Renewal Registrations becomes the standing heading with the January-to-June 1955 issue. ABC Music Corporation leads, its orchestra folio filed under editor Mayhew L. Lake. The alphabet mixes corporate claimants and personal authors without distinction.

Books, pamphlets, serials, and periodical contributions make up the field, under author, issuing body, or title. Variant forms of names get their own cross-references, so a search under one spelling lands at the right heading. Every entry gives original and renewal data together. For anyone tracing whether a 1927 work stayed in copyright, this half-year list is the place the answer was printed in 1955.
u-s-copyright-renewals-1956-january-june:
Wording shifts again in 1956. The first half year's headnote calls the catalog simply a list, arranged by author or issuing body, or by title for serials and compendia. Renewal claimants' cross-references are now described as interfiled, woven into the single alphabet.

Early entries include the Right Reverend Abbot's angels, referred to Anscar Vonier, and George Abbott's play Coquette. Stage work, sermons, and science all renew in the same columns. The entries still give both registrations in full. This half year mostly covers works first copyrighted in 1928, reaching their second term under the old twenty-eight-year rule.
u-s-copyright-renewals-1957-january-june:
A fraternal order's initials, A.M.O.R.C., stand at the head of the January-to-June 1957 alphabet. The headnote now states the arrangement in full: alphabetical under author or issuing body, or by title for serials and certain other works. References from claimants and name variants are interfiled.

That single alphabet serves every kind of printed matter the catalog covers, from occult course materials to trade novels. Entries continue to pair the original registration with the renewal, dates and numbers on both sides. Works of 1929 dominate this half year. Anyone clearing rights in a 1929 book would have started with this list to learn whether its author or publisher renewed.
u-s-copyright-renewals-1958-january-june:
Legal publishing opens 1958's first half, under a heading beginning A.L.R., the American Law Reports line of digests and indexes. Such cumulative legal tools were renewed volume by volume, and their entries recur across these catalogs. The arrangement stays one alphabet of authors and issuing bodies, serials by title.

Books, pamphlets, serials, and periodical contributions fill the issue, each entry carrying original and renewal facts together. References from claimants, joint authors, and editors are interfiled with the main headings. The half year chiefly renews works of 1930. Law firms' libraries depended on these renewals, since a lapsed digest volume complicated citation work for decades.
u-s-copyright-renewals-1959-january-june:
A.M.O.R.C. returns to the head of the alphabet in January-to-June 1959, as it did two years earlier. The Rosicrucian order's course materials were renewed in steady batches, giving the initials a recurring first place. The catalog around it covers the usual field of books, pamphlets, and serials.

Arrangement remains alphabetical under author or issuing body, serials by title, with references interfiled. Both registrations appear in each entry. Most works here were first copyrighted in 1931 and reached renewal in the first half of 1959. The sameness of the form across years is itself the point: a searcher learns one system and can use every volume.
u-s-copyright-renewals-1960-january-june:
Spaced initials, A. M. O. R. C., lead the January-to-June 1960 alphabet. The year's catalogs keep the settled form: books, pamphlets, serials, and periodical contributions, arranged under author or issuing body. Serials and certain other works file by title instead.

References from renewal claimants, joint authors, and editors are interfiled with the headings, and each entry reports both registrations. Works first copyrighted in 1932 supply most entries, their renewal year having arrived. This half year is one of the two real 1960 lists, the year's whole-year record in the set being only a placeholder pointing here and to the autumn issue.
u-s-copyright-renewals-1961-january-june:
A longer headnote introduces January-to-June 1961. Beyond the usual statement of arrangement, it begins a further note on certain registrations, a sign of the catalog's growing fine print. The alphabet itself runs under author or issuing body, serials by title, references interfiled.

Entries give original and renewal registration data side by side, as before. The works renewed this half year date chiefly from 1933. By 1961 the renewal system was a routine of the publishing trade, and the catalog's steady form reflects that routine. Estate executors, corporate successors, and authors themselves all appear as claimants in these columns.
u-s-copyright-renewals-1962-january-june:
The initials A.M.O.R.C. open 1962's first half, marking another batch of the order's renewed course materials. Around them the catalog lists books, pamphlets, serials, and periodical contributions in the usual single alphabet. Authors and issuing bodies head the entries, serials go by title.

Interfiled references lead from claimants, joint authors, and editors to the main headings. Each entry carries both registrations, original and renewal, with their numbers and dates.
